News.title: Naples earthquake live: Italy struck by 4.7 magnitude quake as rocks crush cars
News.content:
Further earthquakes could occur due to seismic activity

People are being warned that further strong earthquakes greater than a magnitude of three could still occur due to seismic activity.

Nello Musumeci, Minister of Civil Protection and Maritime Policies said: "The seismic swarm, as volcanologists tell us, is still ongoing. Therefore, further events with a magnitude greater than 3 could occur.

"Under these conditions, everyone needs to be cautious and self-controlled.

"At present, eight buildings and five businesses have been declared uninhabitable, with 130 families evacuated, equivalent to approximately 290 people; many of them have been sheltered in the areas set up by the municipalities of Naples and Pozzuoli. Five people have been hospitalized for trauma and fractures."

News.title: Headset urgent recall issued over 'serious risk of hearing loss'
News.content:
Headset urgent recall issued over 'serious risk of hearing loss'

Certain batches could emit feedback which may damage your hearing

View Image A product recall has been issued

An urgent safety recall has been issued for a headset over concerns that it could damage people's hearing. The 3M Peltor Comtac VIII Headset has been recalled over concerns about feedback noise.

‌



The headset is designed to give 'critical radio communications' for people in combat and combat support operations. Made in Sweden, it is described as 'over the ear hearing protection and communications headset designed for military and civil defence personnel'.

‌



But there are fears that it could emit feedback noise that will damage people's hearing. The full warning reads: "The product presents a serious risk of hearing loss because affected batches may emit feedback noise (measured up to 106 dBA) through the headset speakers.

‌



"The likelihood of occurrence of this issue can be increased in cold ambient temperatures and with a depleted battery state. The product does not meet the requirements of the Regulation (EU) 2016/425 on Personal Protective Equipment and the applicable standards: EN 352-1:2020, EN 352-4:2020, EN 352-6:2020."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Article continues below

The recall notice states that the product has been recalled from distributors by 3M United Kingdom PLC. A Stop Use Notification has been issued. The recall is applicable to headsets manufactured between November 27 2025 and February 6 2026.

The model numbers that are affected are MT14H418A-02, MT14H418A-35, MT14H418A-38, MT14H418A-86, MT14H418A-87, and MT14H418A-90. the recall notice was issued on Wednesday, July 29.

The recall notice has been issued by the Office for Product Safety & Standards. The lead authority is the Health and Safety Executive, and the PSD case number is 2607-0161.

News.title: Death toll in Spain’s Ceuta border crisis rises as tens of thousands return to Morocco
News.content:
Death toll in Spain’s Ceuta border crisis rises as tens of thousands return to Morocco

Up to 60,000 migrants entered the Spanish territory this week, with dozens dying including some who drowned or were killed in a stampede to cross a breakwater barrier

View 4 Images Spanish soldiers assist a migrant who swam from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug 1, 2026 (Image: AP Photo/Antonio Sempere)

The death toll in Spain’s border crisis with Morocco has risen to 67 with after tens of thousands of migrants entered the tiny enclave of Ceuta in north Africa.

‌



In the unfolding chaos, some people drowned or were killed in a deadly stampede. Spain announced it was installing a 500-metre containment barrier on the sea border between its territory and neighbouring Morocco. It comes after up to 60,000 migrants breached the border earlier this week.

‌



Last month, Spain’s Supreme court ruled migrants arriving by sea to Ceuta could not be summarily deported. A handful of exhausted migrants who swam to Ceuta's urban Tarajal beach on Saturday morning were met by soldiers who escorted them back across the border.

‌



Major EU airport to close for days for runway repairs - all flights cancelled READ MORE :

View 4 Images A Spanish soldier uses a megaphone to speak to migrants sitting on the pavement prior to escorting them back to Morocco, in Spain's north Africa's Ceuta enclave on August 1, 2026 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Spain's interior ministry says the majority of those who entered the territory have already returned to Morocco, claiming that 53,000 of the 60,000 who crossed have now gone back. In Ceuta on Saturday, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said: "We are relentless against those who break the law.”

Questioned how this massive border breach could have happened given the heavy security on both sides of the border and whether Morocco posed a threat to Ceuta, Marlaska defended the government in Rabat. He said: "The events require an evaluation by Spain and Morocco."

‌



But it was the cooperation with its neighbours that allowed Spain "to revert the situation in 24 hours”. Marlaska said: "Morocco is not a threat to Ceuta, or to the rest of Spain. It is a reliable partner."

View 4 Images Spanish soldiers stand next to migrants who swam from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026 (Image: AP Photo/Antonio Sempere)

After days of chaos and streets packed with people who had hoped for a better life in Spain, residents of Ceuta woke up Saturday to an uneasy calm. Even so, security in the autonomous city of 84,000 remained bruised. Ceuta's President Juan Jesus Vivas said: "Life in this city has been disrupted as a result of the border incident.” He added: "The return of people has begun satisfactorily but the process must be completed," he said.

‌



In the Moroccan city of Tangier, about 46 miles west of Ceuta, the main railway station was busy with people returning from Ceuta or the border. Some slept on the ground, exhausted, as passers-by watched from a distance. Aspiring migrant Abdalah said: "I tried to cross, but I failed. I stayed near the border with Ceuta for two days, but I couldn't find anything to eat.”

View 4 Images Spanish soldiers watch migrants sitting on the pavement prior to escorting them back to Morocco, in Spain's north Africa's Ceuta enclave on August 1, 2026 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

On the road leading to the Moroccan town of Fnideq, which borders Ceuta, many migrants were seen walking toward the fence, some barefoot, apparently hoping to try their luck. Taxi drivers and bus operators were refusing to take them, fearing retaliation from authorities. Police officers were deployed along the road, stopping and checking every vehicle heading toward Fnideq.

Article continues below

But some who made it to Ceuta were determined to stay, among them 23-year-old Moroccan Mohamed Hatri. He explained: "They've closed everything down so that we can't buy anything to eat, to force us to return to our country.” He added: "But even if they close it down - we're round to stay here, whether we're hungry or not."

News.title: Legendary mountaineer and ex-British soldier Nirmal Purja confirmed killed in Pakistan avalanche
News.content:
Legendary mountaineer and ex-British soldier Nirmal Purja confirmed killed in Pakistan avalanche

Nirmal Purja, a world famous mountaineer and former Royal Marines soldier has died in Pakistan after an avalanche, while leading an expedition of 10 climbers

View 4 Images Nirmal Purja has died in Pakistan

A world famous mountaineer and former Royal Marines soldier has died in Pakistan after an avalanche.

‌



The company co-founded by Nirmal Purja has confirmed that the Nepalese climber was leading an expedition of 10 climbers on Broad Peak – the world’s 12th highest mountain – in the north of the country when the avalanche struck at about midday on Thursday.

‌



Following search efforts, his company Elite Exped has now confirmed Mr Purja has tragically been killed.

‌



In a post shared on Instagram, the company said: “Today, it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja, tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak. We have also received confirmation that other members of this expedition sadly did not survive.

View 4 Images Purja was a world famous mountaineer (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump gives curt answer to question about Gianni Infantino's FIFA World Cup selloff READ MORE :

“Today, we mourn not only Nims, but every life lost in this tragedy including his trusted climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta) and Nima Sherpa.

‌



“Our deepest thoughts, prayers and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and loved ones. No words can erase the pain of this unimaginable loss, and we ask that everyone respects their privacy as they grieve.”

Pakistani officials previously said the bodies of three climbers - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - who were also on expedition had been recovered.

Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said on social media that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us".

‌



He added: "The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring."

View 4 Images Purja climbed all 14 of the world’s mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days

British adventurer Bear Grylls also paid tribute to Purja, writing on Instagram: “Heartbreaking news for so many climbers around the world who had a relationship with this remarkable and unique man. We will never forget you Nims and your unstoppable spirit.”

‌



Along with Grylls, Purja was enlisted by former Made in Chelsea star Spencer Matthews to help recover the body of his brother Michael, the youngest Briton to summit Everest who disappeared on the mountain in 1999.

Their efforts were captured in the documentary Finding Michael, which was released in 2023. Earlier on Saturday, Matthews said he was praying “for a miracle”.

Matthews shared a photo with the mountaineer on Instagram and said the news from Broad Peak was “heartbreaking”. The 37-year-old said in the post: “The mountains inspire us with their beauty but they also demand immense respect.

‌



“Every person who ventures into that world understands the risks, yet they go anyway, driven by curiosity, purpose, passion and a deep love for the places few will ever experience.

View 4 Images The avalanche happened on Broad Peak (Image: Getty Images)

“The news from Broad Peak is heartbreaking. So many lives, families, friends and teammates now facing unimaginable loss. Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragedy. May those who have been lost be remembered not only for how they died, but for how they lived, the courage they showed, and the lived they touched. Rest in peace. To those not yet found, we pray for a miracle.”

‌



Purja rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world’s mountains with peaks above 8,000 metres (26,247ft) in 189 days – smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

The challenge was the focus of a Netflix documentary called 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible. Purja, 43, powered to the top of the mountains, each with peaks in the so-called “death zone”, starting with Annapurna on April 23 2019 and taking in Everest in May and K2 in July.

He served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

Article continues below

The cold weather warfare specialist said he was the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military. In 2016, he broke mountaineering conventions to rescue a climber left in the “Everest death zone”, bringing her to safety alone.

News.title: 'I represented Huw Edwards - our second meeting left me concerned'
News.content:
'I represented Huw Edwards - our second meeting left me concerned'

Barry Tomes offered to represent fallen newsreader Huw Edwards on a pro bono basis for seven days. After their second meeting, he knew he never wanted to work with him again

View 10 Images Huw Edwards' former publicist Barry Tomes has opened up about the moment he knew he couldn't represent the former star long-term (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Having worked in the publicity business for 54 years, nothing much fazes Barry Tomes, who took on a seemingly impossible task earlier this year by choosing to represent disgraced newsreader Huw Edwards.

Now, the 70-year-old publicist has opened up about the moment he knew he wouldn't be able to work for the former BBC star, and why he now won't pick up the phone to him.

Over his lengthy career, Tomes has represented a number of high-profile clients, from Lulu to The Beach Boys. In recent years, he's carved out a niche by attracting more 'outrageous' talent. This includes Deirdre 'White Dee' Kelly, who rose to fame on the highly controversial 2014 Channel 4 doc Benefits Street, which followed the lives of claimants in Birmingham's Winson Green area.

Other clients include Andrew Wardle, who, due to a rare condition, was born without a penis. In 2018, Andrew, who has spoken openly about his struggles, underwent a £50,000 genital reconstruction surgery, which fitted him with a penile mechanical implant.

Barry was the one who approached Edwards, around one year before the Channel 5 drama Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards was released. As explained to The Mirror, he did so because he was pulling together a case study about mental illness.

View 10 Images The publicist approached Edwards following his shock downfall (Image: TomesPR)

Having sadly lost his grandfather to suicide, as well as friends and colleagues in the music industry, Barry was left with unanswered questions.

He previously started a podcast called Medical Protocols, which connects him with doctors and specialists, where he explores health conditions. In the future, he intends to film a documentary but says this has been a "long process", and that, for a while, he was sidetracked by "the Edwards storm."

Speaking with the Mirror, he pondered: "Are there different forms of it? What does it create? If you have a bang on the head, I know if you have a stroke, it can change things.

"One of [the case studies] was about paedophiles. Having worked with Gary Glitter years ago, I thought he was a great guy - and of course I'm horrified by him now - but I didn't understand why these people went down that route."

View 10 Images In 2024, Edwards pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of children (Image: PA)

Mental health has been an important part of the conversation surrounding Edwards' crimes. In March, the veteran broadcaster expressed fury over docudrama Power, claiming production company Wonderhood "made no attempt" to contact him.

He also announced plans to share his own version of events in a statement at the time, asserting: "I am making an effort to produce my own account of these terrible events. This is a slow process, given the fragile state of my health. I have been open about my struggle with persistent mental illness over a period of 25 years.

"What is less well known is the severity of that condition, which was managed successfully until the downward spiral which led to an appalling outcome. Mental illness is misunderstood by many, but can never be an excuse for criminality. It can, however, at least help explain why people sometimes behave in shocking and reprehensible ways, and why things fell apart for me in the way they did."

View 10 Images Left with unanswered questions over loved ones' suicides, Barry has a strong interest in mental health (Image: TomesPR)

The sentencing report notes that Edwards has arteriosclerosis, a degenerative neurocognitive disorder which results in the hardening and furring of the arteries, and is associated with behavioural disturbance. The judge considered this condition during sentencing.

While Barry was able to get a direct line for Edwards, the formerly lauded presenter didn't return his calls straight away. Then, about a week before the docudrama aired, Barry received a text message while working in Hong Kong. Edwards wanted to speak with him.

Barry remembered: "He called me at midnight, introduced himself, perfectly polite, and he said, I'd really like to meet with you. Now, I assume that was because he knew three days later the docudrama was coming out and he'd obviously got very nervous. He hadn't spoken to any of the press; he hadn't spoken to anybody."

View 10 Images Channel 5 drama Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards sparked a furious response from the former BBC presenter (Image: ©5 Broadcasting Limited / ©Wonderhood Studios / Photographer: Matt Towers Press Enquiries: press@channel5.com NOTE: Channel 5 images are for the use of Press outlets only. Any blogs requesting access to these images are required to seek approval from Channel 5 directly. Contact press@channel5.com While we will continue to send out the weekly PI booklet every Friday, we have now launched the ViacomCBS Media Hub. This is an all-encompassing press centre where you can find the latest PI, press releases and other relevant information. All Paramount pictures must not me altered or manipulated in anyway.)

By this point, Edwards' once stellar reputation was in tatters. In 2024, Edwards pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of children. He was then handed a six-month sentence, suspended for two years, with another charge of accessing 41 images of children. Seven of those images were classified category A, the most serious category, while two showed victims between the ages of seven and nine years old.

It was a case few publicists would dare to take on. After making the 18-hour journey back to the UK, Barry met with Edwards "somewhere in the south of England". Remembering the moment the former broadcasting giant approached him, Barry recalled: "As he walked towards me, I'm like, 'that's the man off the telly, that's the Huw Edwards that I know'. He doesn't look like he's put on a load of weight; that's the man. We spoke, we shook hands, very courteous, very polite, very grateful for me seeing him."

‌



Before moving ahead with anything, Barry knew he had to make one thing crystal clear, asking him: "'Do you want to be back in the media?' No. Okay, that's good because that's not why I'm here. I'm here about the mental health, and I want to talk to you about that in depth at some point."

View 10 Images Before moving ahead with anything, Barry wanted to make sure that Edwards' aim wasn't to get back into the media (Image: ITV)

This was a matter of days before Power aired, and Barry knew all too well that public attention was about to go "nuclear". Edwards needed no reminding of this.

‌



Picking up on Edwards' "anxious" state, Barry says he knew it wasn't the time to pursue the mental health avenue. He remarked, "Whether you like him or not, he is a human being, and he was very anxious. As a duty of care, I didn't want to push anything."

Barry also made it clear to Edwards that no money would be exchanged, claiming he'd only agreed to work for the former newsreader for one week on a pro bono basis. Those seven days proved eventful, however, with Barry representing Edwards on various high-profile platforms, including Good Morning Britain.

While some might have struggled with the backlash of supporting such a controversial figure, battle-worn Barry didn't let criticism or the various "abusive texts" drag him down. He had reportedly arranged to meet with Edwards seven days after their initial meet-up, but the ex-broadcaster was unable to follow through with their plans.

‌



It would allegedly be three full days later that Edwards was finally able to meet, at the same place as that first introduction. This time around, however, Barry saw a side to Edwards that he claims made him uneasy, and, crucially, unlikely to ever work with him again.

View 10 Images For one week only, Barry represented Edwards on various high-profile platforms, including Good Morning Britain (Image: ITV)

In the ten days since the two men had first shaken hands, Barry had counted some 310 articles about Edwards, and claims as many as 11 TV offers rolled in. While Edwards was keen to give his account of things, Barry was conscious that his one-time client was still serving out his sentence. In his view, this move would only lead to more damage.

‌



Furthermore, as Barry observed, in his opinion, Edwards allegedly showed little regret for others over what he'd done. He explained: "I decided that second time, there's no way I'm going to represent. I didn't see regret. Only for regret, my life's over. I didn't see regret for the people."

He continued: "I have had a saying for years and years. I don't believe you should say sorry; I think you should show it, and I don't think he's shown sorry. He said it, or some spokesperson said it in court. I don't think he said it enough."

View 10 Images Barry says he 'didn't see regret' from Edwards during their second meeting (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publis)

‌



The pair walked away from each other that day, and haven't seen each other since. Barry has confirmed he no longer represents Edwards, whom he regards as "ill-advised". While he might still accept a call from a close friend of Edwards, who acts as a third party, he does not speak with him directly.

In the two years since his downfall, Edwards' once extraordinarily successful life appears virtually unrecognisable. He's swapped the fast-paced BBC studio for seclusion in Wales, but despite everything, he's still fighting to have his voice heard through his new Substack.

It's a venture Barry strongly disapproves of, and he initially thought somebody was "having a joke" when he realised that posts had gone live. Barry predicted: "He's digging a hole for himself. I think he's going to come out of the Substacking much worse."

‌



View 10 Images It's believed Edwards could be 'digging a hole for himself' with his new Substack (Image: BBC)

He continued: "I have said to him: nobody actually cares about your opinion about the new Prime Minister. Nobody actually cares about your opinion about French politics or about the history of Wales. You've committed the worst crime."

In a recent post, Edwards took a philosophical view as he reflected on themes of hatred and truth, writing: "It is the failure to separate the crime from the perpetrator which fuels mindless hatred — a hatred which impedes society's ability to understand why some people behave in ways that are destructive and shameful."

‌



Barry remarked, "He's got that wrong. They don't hate him; they hate what he did." While he abhors what Edwards has done, regarding paedophilia as "worse than murder", he still believes he should "have his say", waiting for a good three years to write the book he is reportedly intent on writing, at a time when his mind is clearer.

View 10 Images While Edwards is reportedly keen to write a book, Barry believes some time is needed (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock)

This book should not be thought of as a way back to Edwards' glory days, however. As Barry put it: "He's a very religious man by all accounts, I think he should have his say if that will make him feel better as a human being, but then should go off and work in the church anonymously. That's my opinion."

‌



A humble life of prayer might well be a shock to the system for someone like Edwards, who has forged a name for himself in the spotlight. Barry pondered: "If I'm honest, I think I'm right in saying that I believe he doesn't want to go back to broadcasting and get his TV job back, but he misses the limelight. I've worked with celebrities since I was 17 years old. I know the ones that want the limelight, and I know the ones that don't. And he does."

Reflecting on whether he believes Edwards feels remorse, Barry clarified: "I felt, in my honest opinion, while I was talking to him, he didn't show regret for what had happened. He said he'd been sorry for it. Now, it wasn't a question I asked; I didn't say, 'Do you regret this?' But I didn't see it.

"I don't know what's going on in his mind, obviously, and he may well have apologised a thousand times, but I've not been in touch with him before. Certainly, during that second meeting with him, I thought, in my honest opinion, that he would have said something, like, 'I really regret doing this, I regret it happening'.

Article continues below

"I've read his latest Substack, and he does say he's shown a lot of remorse, and he regrets it. I was merely referring to my personal opinion of when I was in a meeting with him alone."

Do you have a story to share? Email me at julia.banim@reachplc.com

News.title: Can Meghan Markle rebuild her popularity with the British public? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Can Meghan Markle rebuild her popularity with the British public? Take our poll and have your say

Prince Harry & Meghan Markle brought their kids to the UK in a visit where they reunited with the King but a poll suggests the Duchess is still unpopular with the public - have your say below

View 3 Images Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during a visit to Australia in April (Image: Getty Images)

Meghan Markle made her first significant visit to the UK last month but the Duchess appears to still not popular among the public.

‌



Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet joined their mother as they flew out to meet Prince Harry on his UK trip. The family visited the King's Highgrove Estate, the ancestral home of Princess Diana at the Althorp Estate and the Scottish Highlands.

‌



Despite reuniting with King Charles and Queen Camilla on this trip, at a country retreat, the public appears to have not changed their minds on the Duchess of Sussex. A new poll shows that Meghan is still massively unpopular with Brits.

‌



Meghan Markle will never leave California despite Harry reunion, royal expert claims READ MORE :

Should Harry and Meghan be invited to Balmoral this summer? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

View 3 Images Meghan Markle and Prince Harry during their trip (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

The actress turned Royal only a 22 per cent approval rating - with only Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's being lower. This comes after the July family trip appeared to go without a hitch or controversy while the Sussexes were in the UK.

Have your say here and vote in our Mirror readers' poll

‌



Former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond previously told the Mirror : "Meghan is an intelligent woman. I'm sure she is perfectly aware of her extremely low popularity in the UK. I should imagine she now views it as a lost cause and, in any case, she seems to be far happier with her sunshine life in California."

View 3 Images Meghan Markle shared an images of her family visiting Althorp (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

‌



This comes after Meghan shared snaps of her family trip and even posted a picture of Harry and the kids visited the stately home where Princess Diana is buried. In a post on Instagram, captioned 'Summer Holiday', the Duchess included a picture of Lilibet, Archie and Harry walking throgh the famous tree-lined garden at the Althorp Estate.

Prince Archie and Harry can be seen holding large bouquets of flowers as they walk ahead of Meghan and Princess Lilibet. Diana is buried on an island in the middle of the Oval Lake at her ancestral home.

Harry took Meghan to Princess Diana's grave for the first time on the 25th anniversary of his mother's death. Prince Harry flew to the UK, in July, for events to promote the Invictus Games in Birmingham.

Article continues below

He also visited Birmingham Children's Hospital where he praised the work of the WellChild charity, which he is a patron of. The Duke of Sussex was snapped hugging a nurse and he commended the staff, on this third day of his trip across the pond.

News.title: Woman, 32, 'cut out dad's heart and placed it on his dead body,' court hears
News.content:
Woman, 32, 'cut out dad's heart and placed it on his dead body,' court hears

Serena Dolnics, 32, has been charged with murder after police found the body of her father Gregory, 69, covered in blood with his heart allegedly placed on his stomach

View 3 Images Serena Dolnics has been charged with murder (Image: FACEBOOK)

A woman found "covered in blood" has been accused of killing her dad and surgically removing his heart.

Serena Dolnics, 32, was found by police at a house in Valparaiso, around 50 miles from Chicago, by the body of her father and she has now been charged with murder.

Police rushed to the scene following a reported emergency call over concern for the wellbeing of 69-year-old Gregory Dolnics on Sunday evening - with a call handler told by family member that the daughter had been making “odd statements” when they asked to speak with him.

And while the relative was on the phone to 911, the police received text messages from Serena Dolnics’ boyfriend, who was at the home, saying "Serena was covered in blood" - and he believed she had stabbed her father and might kill herself, the affidavit reportedly said.

View 3 Images Serena Dolnics was at the property where her father's body was discovered (Image: FACEBOOK)

Donald Trump gives curt answer to question about Gianni Infantino's FIFA World Cup selloff READ MORE :

Arriving at the property, police found the boyfriend locked outside and peering in through a mirror they could see dried blood and they were unable to contact Gregory Dolnics

Forcing entry, they found the body of Gregory, who had allegedly suffered slash wounds to the head, face, neck and hands, while his heart had been cut out from his body. "Laying on his stomach was what appeared to be his heart," police wrote in the affidavit, reported by USA Today.

According to an autopsy, all of these injuries had been committed with knives, including incisions made to the ribs to allow the removal of the heart.

View 3 Images Serena Dolnics reportedly denies murder (Image: Porter County Sheriff’s Office)

Dolnics, who was found in a bedroom at the property with blood on her feet, was arrested and taken into custody after being treated at hospital due to injuries to her hands.

According to court documents, Dolnics claimed she suffered the cuts to her hands while gardening, although police maintain that these injuries were consistent with a knife slipping through.

She told detectives that she and her father "get along really well" despite having the occasional "small tiff" that they would quickly move past. She also insisted she had not seen Gregory injured.

Article continues below

Dolnics made an initial court appearance on Thursday (July 30), where she wore a blue suicide-prevention smock and reportedly spoke hesitantly via a video chat link.

She has reportedly pleaded not guilty, although she is not yet believed to have arranged an attorney, and when asked in court about this, she said: "I'll figure it out." A further hearing has been scheduled for August 11.

News.title: 'I moved to France for a taste of Paradise but woke up in an apocalypse'
News.content:
For the past 10 days, I’ve been perilously close to the wildfires of the Gironde - and witnessed my first and France’s first fire cloud. I love France, and the prospect of long, sunny summer days, mild winters, and a gentler pace of life ticked all my boxes when, having worked hard and raised a daughter, I moved here in 2021, with Bordeaux on my doorstep. But I'd never bargained for the extremes of weather.

In June of 2022, I found myself in the eye of a tornado. My house is on a hill, with panoramic views, which is great. But that afternoon winds of 140km/hour battered my house. I had a friend staying. Thank god. Between us we battled against a horizontal sheet of rain that chewed up the garden, blew in and buckled my French doors, and tore tiles off the roof. Total cost of damage 12,000 euros.

Another almighty storm in 2023, again in June, wrought havoc in my commune, destroying vines, bringing down trees. Then came 2024, a year marked by floods. Months and months of rain and more rain saw the banks of several rivers burst, flooding towns, villages, and fields. Now, with the wild fires, it’s crazy. The stats are staggering: 220,000 people evacuated from the Gironde and Landes - the biggest evacuation of people in France since the second world war; 300,000 hectares across Spain and France scorched. And no official assessment of the animals lost.

Whitney Houston fans set to splash cash as star's prized items hit auction block READ MORE :

View 4 Images A startled fox watches as woodland burns (Image: Supplied)

France’s minister for Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, stated that the damage to wildlife in the region would be catastrophic, with significant losses among birds, deer and amphibians. Entire groups of deer have been photographed trapped at the forest's edge. One wildlife officer speaking about areas such as Le Porge, said: “Nothing can survive. The fires came too early, at the height of the breeding season. Birds were nesting, fawns lay hidden in the undergrowth.”

Equally staggering has been the response of the people. Across the nation, we’ve all come together to supply food, clothing and shelter to the victims. Animal rescue centres are co-ordinating their efforts and gathering food, bedding, and medication for lost and wounded animals. Jane Marple, animal rescue veteran and head of a local animal association, told me: “This morning a new part of the inner evacuation zone opened for rescuers. This part of the fire zone has been closed since the fires started. We now have night goggles, as we know many animals will lay low during the day and move in the night.”

My friend and I took animal food to St Thomas de Conac – a small village on the Estuary – where we met Mary with her van half-packed, ready to drive up to Ile d’Oleron. We’ve been told to avoid Bordeaux and head north with provisions. Everyone is pitching in “Bordeaux, we’re coming,” read a post on social media, as a convoy of tractors carrying water tanks joined a motorway into the city. Heading across from the Dordogne came a fleet of ambulances to help with the evacuations.

View 4 Images Karen and Mary loads up animal supplies (Image: Supplied)

Such displays of solidarity and comradeship make me incredibly proud to live in this country that I call home. We are all in this together - well, apart from a few ‘ex-pats’ who have complained that their swimming pools have been damaged by falling ash. Yes, really! I do have some sympathy for those gite owners who have lost bookings. The whole of France is not ablaze. It’s a big country. The advice has only ever been to stay away from the Gironde and do not head south via the A63 into Spain, which is battling its own megafire hell.

If the fires had started 20km north of Bordeaux instead of West, I wouldn’t be writing this. I’d be in an evacuation centre, just like the parc d’exposition, grateful for clothes, food, water – grateful to the firefighters working tirelessly to save lives. Friends of mine who live in Merignac, beside the airport, were evacuated and are still not home. Some German friends are still in the parc d’expostion, waiting to return to their holiday home to collect their belongings. Many of the evacuees were holidaymakers and tourists, but many locals have lost their houses, their pets, their livelihoods.

I live about 30 minutes north of Bordeaux – in the shadow of the megafires. I watched from my back porch as the firecloud headed this way. A fire cloud, or pyrocumulonimbus, happens when a wildfire is so intense it built its own thunderstorm. The cloud creates its own lightning, hurls embers up to 30 km ahead of the fire front, and drives the flames in directions no one can predict.

View 4 Images The dramatic view from Linda's porch (Image: Supplied)

Last Friday, smoke from the Cap Ferat and Biscarosse fires travelled up the Gironde estuary and choked my neighbourhood. The ominous black cloud sat above us for almost 12 hours, dispensing no rain, just bangs and flashes from the thunder and lightning. At 9 o’clock on Saturday morning my neighbours and I were transfixed by the eerie silence that followed. No birds, no wind, just an end-of-the-world glow coming from the south.

As I write, the fires are stable but the smell of smoke still lingers in the air. We suffered temperatures of 42C again yesterday. This is our third big canicule (a period of scorching heat) this year, and each time they last for days or weeks… And still no rain in my commune. My fruit trees have died. All around me, fields of maize and sunflowers are stunted. The grapes are splitting on the vines. Walking in forests is prohibited, so is hunting (no bad thing!).

The French aren’t good with rules. If we see one we like to bend it or break it, but along with the camaraderie I’ve witnessed has come a new respect for nature and the environment. We’ve just received a stark reminder of how fragile it all is. And we are working together to protect it.,My adopted home of south-west France is beautiful, wild and charming – and a million miles away from my former life in London – but I wouldn’t go back no matter what the weather decides to fling at me.

News.title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in Pakistan avalanche, his company says
News.content:
Renowned mountaineer and former British Army soldier Nirmal Purja is among those killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan, his company has said.

Elite Expeditions shared the news on social media, saying it was with "profound sadness and immense heartbreak" that it confirmed Purja's death in Thursday's avalanche.

It also said that the other nine members of the expedition had died.

Purja, a Nepali-born climber, was known for scaling the world's 14 highest peaks in just over six months in 2019.

Pakistani officials previously said the bodies of three climbers - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - who were among the 10-person expedition had been recovered.

Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said on social media that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us".

"The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added.

Rescue teams in Pakistan had been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit.

Purjam 43, became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released in 2021.

The avalanche happened on Thursday on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja, who joined the British Army in 2003 and the Special Boat Service - the Royal Navy's special forces unit - in 2009.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

News.title: Sir John Curtice: The "Burnham bounce" is real but it's not massive
News.content:
But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.

Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons' authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.

This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.

News.title: He thought a fitness supplement was safe, but it sent him into psychosis
News.content:
Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.

But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.

Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.

The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.

The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country.

His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.

Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.

Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.

News.title: What is Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and why does Trump say he wants to bomb it?
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb a suspected underground nuclear site in Iran known as Pickaxe Mountain, where recent satellite images appear to show construction work taking place.

Pickaxe Mountain is one of the few Iranian sites linked to the country's nuclear programme that has not been the target of US and Israeli strikes. There have been unproven claims that some of Iran's stock of highly enriched uranium may be kept there, which could be further enriched for use in nuclear weapons.

"We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily," Trump told reporters on 21 July. And on 28 July he said: "I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe. It's not a big problem - we took out their nuclear sites, and we'll have to take out Pickaxe if we don't make a deal."

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on 22 July that "no nuclear activity is taking place" at Pickaxe Mountain, and described US threats as "a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage".

BBC Verify and BBC Persian have spoken to experts and analysed satellite imagery to piece together what we know about the site, and the potential impact of any strike.

News.title: Decades-long search ends with discovery of new marine species
News.content:
The Great Barrier Reef might be the world's most famous underwater ecosystem, but hidden in UK waters lies an ancient marine world you may not have heard of.

Known as maerl beds, these carpets of coral-like seaweed create some of the richest habitats in the sea.

And 40 years ago, while studying one such bed for her PhD, Prof Christine Maggs found a fragment of pink-striped seaweed living on maerl she had never seen before.

The discovery would become a lifelong obsession and a decades-long scientific puzzle.

News.title: Former workers fight for wages they say they're owed: 'It makes me sick'
News.content:
What happens when your boss is also the HR department, the grievance handler and the person deciding whether you get paid?

"I just want my wages. It's my hard work. I just want what I'm owed."

Sonia Garcia Monuz is one of several workers trying to recover money she believes she is owed by a catering firm based in Berkshire.

Latest figures show early conciliation cases involving unpaid wages rose by about 17% between 2024 and 2025, according to Acas â the independent body that helps resolve workplace disputes.

Acas says nearly half of hospitality workers, 49%, experience problems at work.

News.title: Who is Greater Manchester's new Mayor Bev Craig?
News.content:
Having grown up on a council estate in Belfast, Craig moved to Manchester in 2003 at the age of 18 to study politics and modern history at the University of Manchester.

After graduating, she began her career in local government. She went on to work in higher education and then at a national trade union, leading on social care.

Craig was first elected as a councillor for the Burnage ward on Manchester City Council in 2011.

She was executive member for adult social care and health throughout the Covid-19 global pandemic, before becoming deputy council leader in 2021.

Craig soon took over as leader when Sir Richard Leese stood down after 25 years in the role.

Her promotion made her the local authority's first female boss and the council's first openly gay leader.

The 41-year-old has also held the role of deputy mayor for economy, business and inclusive growth on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

She was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the New Year Honours List in 2025 for services to local government.

News.title: Greater Manchester mayor says Burnham's new powers will change lives
News.content:
Greater Manchester's new mayor Bev Craig has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham's move to give the regions more power could "change our lives".

The Labour candidate claimed victory in Thursday's by-election after securing 309,525 votes over Reform's Sian Astley, who won 157,178.

The 41-year-old will succeed Burnham as mayor, after he stood down to run in the Makerfield by-election in June. The pair appeared together at a Labour rally in Manchester after Craig's election win.

Craig said: "For a prime minister two weeks in, to start giving powers out of Whitehall and putting it in the places that can make a difference - that can change our lives."

She added: "I will rise to his challenge about taking the power and control that he is offering mayors like me to make our regions better.

"Because that is what it is all about."

News.title: Stick to spending limits, PM and chancellor tell ministers in joint memo
News.content:
Healey said the budget would "meet our fiscal rules" and "give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future".

A report in the Times says the joint letter told ministers they must work "within the budgets they have already got" even while "pay[ing] for new things they want to do this year and next".

While the ongoing war in Iran is pushing up inflation and borrowing costs, senior Treasury sources confirmed the government is determined to stay "well within the fiscal rules" inherited from Sir Keir Starmer and his chancellor Rachel Reeves.

But Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

He also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this, and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain should lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

Questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

Reeves left a Â£22bn buffer in her last budget, but persistent inflation due to the Iran war could have eroded it.

On Friday, the PM said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his efforts to move power out of London.

Reeves had previously said that regional mayors could be given control of some tax revenue to spend on their local priorities.

Labour pledged to devolve more powers to local councils and mayors as part of its 2024 election manifesto, in areas such as housing and transport.

More details of Burnham's plan are expected to be announced in the Budget, but the government said the rate of income tax will not change as a direct result of the reforms.

AJ Bell public policy director Tom Selby said Healey "doesn't have the luxury of pointing the finger of blame at the last administration".

"Healey will likely spend a chunk of his time leafing through the thesaurus looking for new ways to rephrase the 'tough choices' message of his predecessor," he said.

Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the announcement of the budget date meant "89 more days of unfunded spending commitments and damaging tax speculation until we get some details".

"89 more days for Brits to wait before they know how much their taxes are going to go up to fund Burnham's spending addiction", he said.

News.title: Soap star Shane Richie facing drink-drive charge
News.content:
EastEnders actor Shane Richie is to appear in court charged with drink-driving, police have said.

Essex Police confirmed it was called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the Church Langley Way area of Harlow, shortly before 23:20 BST on Wednesday.

A force spokesman confirmed the 62-year-old, of Tadworth, Surrey, was arrested and a charge of drink-driving had been authorised against him.

It added Richie, real name Shane Roche, was due to appear at Colchester Magistrates' Court on 9 September.

Richie plays Alfie Moon in EastEnders, making his first appearance in the BBC soap in 2002.

The Sun reported he was arrested, external at a Tesco petrol station forecourt.

Essex Police said: "Officers were called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the area of Church Langley Way, Harlow, shortly before 23:20 on Wednesday, 29 July.

"On arrival, officers arrested a man.

"A charge of drink-driving has subsequently been authorised against Shane Roche, 62, of Tadworth, Surrey."

Richie's representative has been contacted for comment.

News.title: Police arrest men over alleged modern day slavery
News.content:
Two men have been arrested in Kent on suspicion of modern day slavery and money laundering offences.

Dorset Police said the 20-year-old from Sussex and a 22-year-old from Buckinghamshire were arrested during an investigation into suspected exploitation, immigration and financial offences.

Officers made the arrests after raiding a business premises in Gillingham, it added.

Three further men were also arrested for immigration offences, the force continued.

Dorset Police said the raid followed intelligence from the community and detailed enquiries.

The force added that the "day of action" had led to a number of individuals being safeguarded.

News.title: Commonwealth Games boxing official suspended over headbutt probe
News.content:
A boxing official has been banned from serving at the Commonwealth Games over allegations he headbutted a teenage fighter in the ring.

Jon-Paul Hynd also faces claims he struck another child with an unknown object during a training session at Beath Boxing Club in Cowdenbeath, Fife.

Hynd was appointed as a technical official for the games in Glasgow, but Boxing Scotland said he had been suspended pending an investigation.

Beath Boxing Club did not respond when asked for comment by BBC Scotland News.

Complaints lodged with the sport's governing body detail claims Hynd "physically assaulted" one boxer, aged 15, by "striking him with his head" after the fighter responded to "verbal belittlement" last year.

Police Scotland investigated the incident but found no evidence of criminality.

News.title: CPS to target assets of jailed funeral director
News.content:
A disgraced funeral director's bank accounts and assets have been frozen, as prosecutors seek to recover cash fleeced from his victims.

Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years at Hull Crown Court on Friday for 67 offences, including denying 30 people a decent and proper burial and giving families the ashes of strangers.

Bush, 48, who ran Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, stole up to Â£12,000 from charities and sold fake funeral plans.

Laura Tams KC, deputy chief crown prosecutor at the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said: "We will be looking at him, at the financial aspects of this case, to see if we can confiscate any of the proceeds of his crimes and try to compensate the families."

Sentencing Bush following a five-day hearing, Mr Justice Hilliard said it was clear that he "benefited very substantially" and "obviously lived very well".

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Tams said it "was not a case of somebody that had recently fallen on hard times".

She added: "I think the scale of the offending, the length of time it had gone on for, showed that really this had become something of his business model."

News.title: Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulation
News.content:
Tristan Essex is standing on the steps of Hull Crown Court, shoulder to shoulder with several others whose lives have been devastated by disgraced funeral director Robert Bush.

The 27-year-old is fighting alongside his sister Claire for regulation of the funeral industry, a journey that has seen them take their campaign to Downing Street and resulted in a new pledge from the government "to take urgent action to crack down on rogue funeral operators".

Their grandmother Jessie Stockdale was one of Bush's victims â her body one of the 35 found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, five months after her funeral was held.

The news knocked the family off its feet, Tristan said. Even worse, they learned the ashes they had been given were not Jessie's remains.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

News.title: Tortoise that ended up at tip reunited with owner
News.content:
An adventurous tortoise is home safe and well after being rescued from a recycling and garden waste centre.

Arnold ventured into owner Jacqueline Sear's garden waste bag before she was unknowingly taken to St Erth Household Waste and Recycling Centre in Cornwall on Tuesday.

Suez, which runs the facility, sent out emails asking customers who had been at the centre on Tuesday if they had lost a tortoise.

Arnie's owner said she was relieved her "very curious" tortoise was found alive after initially fearing the worst.

News.title: I was in a coma for 42 days after a tick bite on a holiday to Greece
News.content:
A woman has been left with memory loss and seizures and has to take 18 tablets a day after a tick bite on a Greek holiday left her in a coma for nearly six weeks.

Victoria Stellas, from Anglesey, had flu-like symptoms while on the island of Syros in 2019, then - once back home - started having night seizures.

She went to hospital but "no-one knew what was wrong" so had an MRI scan and was flown by helicopter to Liverpool's Walton Centre, external, where she was put in an induced coma for 42 days.

From there Victoria was diagnosed with tick-borne encephalitis, external (TBE), a potentially fatal brain inflammation.

"It's changed my life completely. Apart from the work I don't go out as much," the 51-year-old said.

Mum-of-one Victoria believes she was bitten when she was at her brother-in-law's home as he has goats that can attract ticks.

She said: "I just kept on having seizures and no-one knew what was wrong. It was an unusual infection, and they didn't have the experts I think to diagnose this.

"Altogether it was about six months from when I was in hospital, the treatment afterwards.

"Sometimes I just keep quiet. I was outgoing before."

Victoria said she lost her jobs in a pub and as a teaching assistant at a school for children with special educational needs and disabilities, due to her symptoms.

News.content:

More than half of Britons would rather brave the cold than suffer through the heat currently gripping the UK, new polling has shown.

A survey of 2,000 adults found that 52 per cent of the nation prefer colder conditions, while just 28 per cent would rather be warm.

People who favour cooler temperatures say they sleep better, hate feeling sweaty, and are more irritable in the heat, according to drinks brand Minus 196.

Laurence Wainwright, a senior lecturer at the University of Oxford, said people often prefer cooler weather because it is easier to regulate body temperature.

“With cool weather, we can control that to some degree,” he said.

“[In the UK], only about 5 per cent of homes have air conditioning...there's only so many layers you take off when it when it's hot.”

open image in gallery More than half of those who prefer to be cold say it is because it is easier to sleep ( Getty )

Around 65 per cent of those who prefer to be cold say it is because they get better sleep, the poll revealed.

“I think the public are aware of the impacts that heat has on sleep, and it's very fresh in their memory from what's happened the last couple of months,” he added.

The research comes as the UK suffers through its fourth heatwave this year, with wildfires devastating large swathes of land across the country.

Some 63 per cent of people who prefer the cold said it was because they hated being sweaty, while 50 per cent say it is because they are more irritable when hot.

“The body has limited resources to do almost unlimited things, so it has to make trade-offs,” Mr Wainwright said. “It has to make tough decisions, and when it's overheated, it says, ‘this is a high-level risk, we have to put all of our resources into cooling down’.

“As a result, some of those higher-order cognitive functions, like the ability to have an empathetic, thoughtful conversation with a partner, go out the window.”

open image in gallery Around 30 per cent of Britons will avoid public transport in the extreme heat ( PA Archive )

Mr Wainwright said hotter temperatures can also be detrimental for people with mental health conditions.

“For those with an existing condition, symptoms are worsened, and new symptoms can manifest. The medications cause a whole range of different problems...side effects, particularly sweating, can be exacerbated.

“For those taking antipsychotics, like those with bipolar and schizophrenia, antipsychotics actually interfere with the ability of the body to thermoregulate. For those taking stimulants for ADHD, sleep is significantly impacted.”

He added: “For the entire country, we know that poor sleep is directly correlated with poorer mental health outcomes.”

The research also found that during a heatwave, 44 per cent of Britons will avoid exercise, 39 per cent will steer clear of household chores, and 38 per cent will not go outside.

Some 30 per cent say they will also avoid public transport if it is too hot.

A spokesperson for Minus 196 said: “Everyone has their own way of getting through the heat, whether that’s reaching for a cold drink, sitting in front of a fan or simply avoiding anything too strenuous.

“Heat can affect everything from sleep and productivity to our social lives, meaning most feel they function better when things are a little cooler.”

When Robert Downey Jr. appeared at San Diego Comic-Con earlier this week to discuss the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, eagle-eyed fans quickly spotted that his outfit appeared to contain a hidden message.

The 61-year-old actor, who helped launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe in his role as Iron Man, will this time be taking on the very different role of villain Doctor Doom. At Comic-Con, he wore a custom jacket embroidered with a series of mysterious runes.

Now, one dedicated fan on Reddit believes they have been able to decipher the coded message.

The user, who posts under the name EditWithEgo, used various other pieces of Avengers: Doomsday marketing in order to deduce that the runes are a “phonetic cipher of English.”

If their theory is correct, the runes over the jacket’s right pocket read “Revenge” while the message over the left pocket reads: “Justice.”

open image in gallery Robert Downey Jr. wearing a jacket covered in runes at an 'Avengers: Doomsday' event at San Diego Comic-Con in July 2026 ( Getty )

Meanwhile, the runes on the jacket’s lapel spell out: “There is no promise of tomorrow.”

The right cuff reads: “To the victor,” while the left cuff, which is only partially visible in photos, appears to complete the phrase: “Go the spoils.”

“To the victor, go the spoils,” is a popular political saying that dates back to at least the 1800s, and in this case is also a pun: in Marvel Comics, Doctor Doom’s full name is Dr. Victor Werner von Doom.

The runes, which in Marvel lore originate from Latveria, the fictional European country that Doctor Doom rules over, are expected to play a deeper role in Avengers: Doomsday. They also appear on the armour that Doom wears in the film.

open image in gallery The first in the two-part Avengers finale is set for release on December 18 ( Getty )

Marvel fans got a better look at the forthcoming superhero film when an extended trailer premiered at Comic-Con.

The trailer emphasises Doctor Doom’s relationship with the Fantastic Four, making it clear that Pedro Pascal’s Mr Fantastic and the rest of the group have a troubled pre-existing relationship with the villain.

The footage was shown only to Hall H attendees at Comic-Con and is not yet available online. It follows the release of a first trailer last week, which fans branded “disappointing”.

Fans who have seen both appear to prefer the second, with many questioning why Marvel didn’t lead with it.

“OK, the second Doomsday trailer is so much better than the first,” wrote one person on X, with another echoing the same sentiment: “Why wasn’t this the first Doomsday trailer cause it’s way better than whatever that slop first trailer was.”

The forthcoming film, the first in a two-part Avengers finale, will feature almost every major character from the MCU. It’ll be released on 18 December – the same day as Dune: Part 3.

When she was 10 years old, Ayesha received a call from her father. It was Friday afternoon, and he had gone to pray at the mosque as usual, but this time he had called to say the building was under attack.

An hour after that call, Ayesha’s family learnt that her father had been shot in the head, with shrapnel wounding his abdomen. The attackers had even opened fire at the ambulance he was in, but the driver managed to get them to safety. Her brother, meanwhile, had sought refuge in the mosque’s basement.

Ayesha’s family are Ahmadi Muslims, a minority reformist movement within Islam who face severe persecution in countries such as Pakistan, where Ayesha is from.

On 28 May 2010, terrorists from Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan attacked two Ahmadi mosques in Lahore, killing 94 people and injuring over 100 others, including Ayesha’s father.

open image in gallery Hazrat Mirza Masroor Ahmad, worldwide head of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, described the Jalsa Salana convention as ‘a living example of Islam’s peaceful teachings in practice’ ( Ahmadiyya Muslim Community )

Everything changed for Ayesha after the attack. Her friends at school discovered she was an Ahmadi Muslim, which she had previously managed to keep private. Her teachers began treating her differently: her English teacher told her she should become “a real Muslim”, while another teacher was overheard saying “animals were better” than Ahmadis.

The turning point came a year after the mosque attacks, when her family home in Lahore was directly targeted by gunmen who were shooting from close range.

Now 26, Ayesha, whose family sought refuge in the UK over a decade ago, was one of the thousands of Ahmadi Muslims who gathered in Alton, Hampshire, last weekend for Jalsa Salana, the UK’s largest Islamic gathering. The gathering, run by the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, marked its 60th year.

Ayesha describes the event as “liberating”. Members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community travel from across the UK and abroad to hear addresses by His Holiness Hazrat Mirza Masroor Ahmad, worldwide head of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community.

The event is also attended by MPs, bishops, local councillors and faith leaders, with heightened security measures in place after safety concerns caused a religious convention in Suffolk to end early.

Maria Sadaf, 31, also left Pakistan after her family faced religious persecution. Her religious studies teacher at school would regularly tell the class there was an “infidel” present. At Jalsa Salana, she volunteers in hospitality.

“I work behind the scenes at Jalsa, but I have never felt more seen somehow,” she tells The Independent. “There’s something about quietly sorting out a queue, or walking a stranger to her seat, knowing nobody will ever know it was me.

“And I think that’s exactly how service before God is meant to feel. It’s not for anyone to see. It’s between me and Him.

“I lose myself in something much bigger than me for those few days, and that’s when I feel most sure of who I actually am.”

Saira Bhatti, 25, has been attending the event for as long as she can remember. A few weeks ago, when visiting the seaside in Bournemouth with her friends, she was confronted by a woman who questioned why they were dressed “like that”. Born and raised in the UK, the experience shook Saira who was left unsettled by the remarks.

As a visibly Muslim woman, she believes Jalsa Salana offers a sanctuary she cannot find elsewhere: “For me, Jalsa is one of the few places where I put all of that down.

open image in gallery Volunteers Saira Bhatti (left) and Bareera Ghaffar find the women’s space at Jalsa Salana empowering ( Bareera Ghaffar )

“Surrounded by thousands of women from different generations and walks of life, I’m not thinking about how I look or how I’m being perceived. I’m simply present.”

Bareera Ghaffar, 27, a global mental health researcher, feels the event comes at a time when many are actively seeking genuine community: “Padel and run clubs are on the rise, and there is the discussion about the need for third spaces. Community is more important now than ever, and this is where spaces like Jalsa Salana come in.”

Jalsa Salana is segregated, with women from the community running their half of the vast site, often described as a “tent city”.

Speaking to The Independent, Dr Fariha Khan, a GP from Surrey, says: “His Holiness has spoken about how women truly flourish outside the shadow of men, and for me Jalsa Salana is the proof. At the convention, we see everyone from young girls to older ladies playing their part in running this huge event. And the result is brilliant.

“There is a finesse, a thoughtfulness and deep care that you find on the ladies’ side at Jalsa Salana – and that comes from it being a women’s space.”

open image in gallery Thousands of women volunteer at the Jalsa Salana convention each year ( Bareera Ghaffar )

The event has an open kitchen serving meals three times a day to thousands of attendees. Hala Hadi, 22, who volunteers in the dining marquee, is drawn to the women’s-only space: “Women are so often lost in the imagination of others before they are encountered as distinct individuals,” she says.

Ayesha Malik, a human rights lawyer who has spoken out against extremism, believes this event helps promote a positive understanding of women’s rights in Islam by encouraging equal participation.

“This space is our sanctuary – a separation from men that denotes strength rather than weakness: women are not ‘separated’ but ‘separate and distinct’ from men,” she says.

“Jalsa Salana is not just about a space that is for ‘only women’; it epitomises what ‘only women’ can achieve when they come together as a community and wear all their hats: mothers, wives, daughters, friends, humans.”

Police action against supporters of the recent Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protests has reportedly intensified, with activists alleging a nationwide crackdown on people who participated in the 36-day agitation.

A case has been opened against a woman identified by police as 25-year-old Ruchika Singh for allegedly using "abusive and objectionable" language against prime minister Narendra Modi during the youth-led protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 23 July.

After her image was plastered across Indian media amid police claims that she was on the run, on Saturday a video purporting to be from Singh was posted to social media, apologising “to the entire nation” for “saying a lot of things”. She claimed she was just 15, not 25, and that she had been “influenced” by other protesters.

Meanwhile, police in the southern Indian city of Hyderabad registered a case against Meta India’s head over Facebook posts that “depicted Mr Modi in an abusive manner”, a police official said on Friday.

Authorities are preparing to write to Meta as part of the investigation, V Aravind Babu, Hyderabad’s deputy commissioner of police for cyber crimes, said, according to Reuters.

The complaints allege that the manipulated content was derogatory, misleading, and capable of inciting public disorder.

Meta did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment on Friday. The case ‌adds to a string of ‌tensions between Meta and Modi's government over content tied to the prime minister. India's IT ministry summoned Meta executives ⁠this week after Facebook briefly restricted Mr Modi’s post last week, with a top official saying the government wanted Meta to explain the matter at the highest level.

A Meta spokesperson said at the time that the post, which was Mr Modi's first where he addressed massive student protests that forced the resignation of the education minister, had been blocked inadvertently. Mr Modi has also come in for a ⁠barrage of online criticism, jokes and ridicule by protesters in ‌recent weeks.

Protesters have said that authorities intensified detentions in the weeks following the agitation that forced the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

One of the protest’s best-known volunteers, 24-year-old law student Mohammad Junaid, approached the Supreme Court alleging that he was illegally detained, interrogated overnight and released the following day because of his role in organising the demonstrations.

In his petition, he has also alleged that police questioned his father and searched the family’s home. Ghaziabad Police have denied the allegations relating to the search, saying only that his father was questioned, the BBC reported.

Civil liberties groups and opposition leaders have criticised the police action, while CJP leaders have accused authorities of targeting volunteers after the protests ended.

The Delhi Police has not publicly responded to Mr Junaid’s allegations.

On Thursday, Delhi Police said no legal action would be taken against people who took part in the recent protests, provided they did not have a criminal record, according to News18.

The CJP is a youth-led satirical movement whose logo is an outline of a cockroach on a mobile phone. The group's 30-year-old founder, ​Abhijeet Dipke, says CJP was so named because of comments by Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant comparing some unemployed youth to cockroaches. Kant later said ​he did not mean to criticise young people but was referring to those with “fake and bogus degrees” who were “like parasites”.

CJP spokesperson, Saurav Das, distanced the organisation from the alleged use of abusive language during the protests but criticised the use of criminal law against demonstrators.

“If any language used was derogatory in nature, then the person concerned is free to pursue civil and criminal defamation proceedings against the individual concerned. However, the use of the criminal justice machinery against protesters is highly condemnable, and no one should be punished merely for using objectionable language,” Mr Das was quoted as saying by Indian newswire Press Trust of India.

“The language may be wrong, and it may be objectionable to someone, but that is no reason to invoke the criminal justice machinery against such people. It creates a chilling effect. I don’t think this is acceptable to anybody, especially the younger generation,” he said.

“I would request the younger generation to be very careful about the words they use and the kind of insults or remarks they make against people in general,” he said.

Opposition Congress president and leader of opposition in upper house of parliament, Mallikarjun Kharge, called for the resignation of home minister Amit Shah over the police crackdown on CJP’s protests.

On Tuesday, India’s Supreme Court ordered the release of minors arrested during the protests and directed authorities to preserve CCTV footage after petitioners alleged police used excessive force against demonstrators.

Indian media reported that Mr Kant also ordered officials to preserve the digital and personal data of protesters and barred any coercive action against those who took part in the protests.

The reports said Mr Kant took interim steps in response to petitions filed by student protesters and activists seeking ​action against police and paramilitary forces for what they said was the use of excess force ⁠and pellet guns during the weeks-long demonstrations.

The government has, meanwhile, defended the police response, saying officers acted within the law to control the protests.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the Supreme Court that allegations of students being assaulted were serious, but said around 250 police personnel were also injured.

The protests, triggered by the leak of question papers for a national medical college entrance exam, ended on Saturday after the education minister resigned and the government agreed to the protesters' demands for exam reforms, withdrawal of police cases, and compensation ​for families of students who died by ​suicide after the leaks.

Icelandic coast guards and special forces seized a ship operated by a group founded by anti-whaling activist Paul Watson and detained its crew, officials in the Arctic island nation said Saturday.

The Icelandic Coast Guard said the crew of whaling ship Hvalur 9 requested assistance on Thursday evening because they believed their safety was under threat from the protest vessel Bandero. It said the Bandero ignored coast guards’ instructions to leave Icelandic waters, and later an order to stop its engines.

Coast guards and the police special forces Viking Squad boarded the vessel around midnight on Thursday and detained its crew. Watson was not aboard.

The Captain Paul Watson Foundation confirmed in a statement that the vessel had been seized. It said the 21 crew members were being detained aboard the ship without their phones.

The ship arrived Friday in Reykjavik, Iceland’s capital, and police have taken over the investigation, the coast guard agency said. Icelandic national broadcaster RUV reported that police will seek to deport the crew and ban them from returning to Iceland.

Along with Norway and Japan, Iceland is one of the only countries still practicing commercial whaling.

The country sets annual quotas for the fin whales and minke whales fishermen are allowed to hunt in its waters. It exports most of its whale meat to Japan, but demand there has dwindled since Japan left the IWC and resumed commercial whaling in 2019.

The hunt is increasingly contentious in Iceland, where whale meat is now rarely eaten.

Canada-born Watson, 75, is a former head of the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, whose high seas confrontations with whaling vessels have drawn support from celebrities, featured in the reality television series “Whale Wars” and regularly landed him in jail. He left Sea Shepherd in 2022 to set up his foundation.

Watson was imprisoned in Greenland for five months in 2024 after being arrested on a Japanese warrant over charges of obstructing a whaling ship in 2010. On his release in December 2024, Watson said he would be careful not to be caught again.

“I have to make sure that I don’t land in Iceland or another country where Interpol might try to have me arrested again,” he said

In 2012, Watson was made the subject of a “red notice” by the international police organization Interpol. He was removed from the most-wanted list in 2025.

His hard-line tactics have split the movement he started, and marine firms have accused the anti-whaling activists of endangering vessels and lives.

Earlier this year, the Bandero collided with an industrial krill trawler in Antarctica in what the ship’s Norwegian owner said was a deliberate attack that endangered its crew and could have caused an environmental disaster.
