Sports.title: Tottenham star suffers pre-season nightmare as he is sent off just THREE minutes after being subbed on in calamitous outing against Chelsea
Sports.content:
Tottenham star Kevin Danso endured a brief pre-season nightmare after he was sent off against bitter Premier League rivals Chelsea in Sydney on Saturday.

The defender was brought on by manager Roberto De Zerbi during the clash after half-time, with the two teams all square at 1-1 after the first-half.

But after just three minutes, he was handed his marching orders for a risky and unnecessary challenge on a sprinting Joao Pedro.

Danso was the last line of defence as the Brazilian striker pounced on an inexpert pass backwards, and as Pedro made for the goal, the Austrian dragged him down in a rush of blood to the head.

Little time was wasted as the referee produced a red card, with Chelsea handed a freekick from 30 yards - as Danso trudged down the tunnel towards the Tottenham dressing room.

Chelsea's partisan commentary team pointed out that Danso had been a 'silly boy' not to let Pedro run through and face the consequences, as the two teams were hardly playing a critical league tie at Stadium Australia.

Kevin Danso saw red as Tottenham met Premier League rivals Chelsea in a pre-season friendly

The Austrian defender skittled Joao Pedro as he pounced on a loose pass and headed for goal

The Spurs star spent just three minutes on the pitch after being introduced at half-time

Spurs had been the team to open the scoring courtesy of an opening goal for new £100million midfielder Sandro Tonali.

The former Newcastle star put away his team's first shot on target in the match, his strike bamboozling Chelsea's young goalkeeper Teddy Sharman-Lowe.

But just four minutes later in the 21st minute, Estevao brought the tie level with a neat finish, the west London faithful no doubt delighted to see the starlet back in the goals after the latter stages of his 2025-26 season hampered by injury.

With his side down to 10 men as the second-half ticked on, Spurs goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky was forced to make a number of excellent saves as Chelsea threw the kitchen sink at their London rivals.

But Tottenham continued to cling on, with the score level heading into the final 20 minutes - before Richarlison snatched the winner with a rebounded effort to make it 2-1 Down Under, and hand Spurs the Sydney Super Cup.

Chelsea and Spurs' entanglements are typically heated, with neither team unfamiliar with receiving handfuls of bookings when they meet on English soil.

Tottenham were memorably reduced to nine men during one recent meeting, which saw Chelsea see out a 4-1 win against Ange Postecoglou's side in November 2023.

Sports.title: 'Some **** from doping is here': How expletive-ridden text messages and a dog walk led to former Wimbledon champion landing a FOUR-YEAR drugs ban
Sports.content:
Former Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova referred to a doping control officer (DCO) as a '****' and took her dog for a walk after refusing a drugs test which led to a four-year ban from tennis, the tribunal's full written decision on the case has revealed.

Shockwaves were sent through the sport in late June when the 2023 champion was handed the jaw-dropping sanction for barring the DCO from administering a test at her home in Prague at 8pm in December 2025.

Vondrousova claimed that she had been concerned for her safety and suffered 'an acute stress reaction' which had hampered her decision-making, prompting her to sign a document offered by the DCO confirming her refusal.

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) stressed in their decision to sanction the Czech star to the fullest extent came from wanting to ensure the length of a ban refusing a test is the same as testing positive.

'This is to ensure that anyone who is doping cannot serve a shorter ban simply by refusing to be tested,' The ITIA's initial statement confirmed.

The release of Friday's written decisions in full has revealed that the extent to which Vondrousova was deemed to have deliberately refused the test by the independent tribunal.

The full written reasons as to why Marketa Vondrousova received a four-year ban from tennis have been published

'This is a very unfortunate manner in which the player made a decision in the heat of the moment to refuse doping control, in a state of stress and anxiety, with significant consequences,' the tribunal said on Friday, adding that she had not offered 'compelling justification' for refusing the test.

The 26-year-old's defence was threefold: that she had felt unsafe by the arrival of a DCO outside of her dedicated testing window; that the DCO had not followed procedure and had not identified herself to Vondrousova, adding to the threat she felt; and that her decision-making had been impaired by her anxiety and the 'acute stress reaction' which overcame her.

But findings from Vondrousova's WhatsApp messages showed that she had been quick to understand that the DCO was here to test her outside of her requested window when the officer first rang her doorbell and announced herself.

'So like here is ringing some **** from the doping,' Vondrousova messaged her boyfriend, fellow Czech player Andrew Paulson, after first refusing the DCO entry to her apartment, and speaking on the phone to her agent Enric Molina.

Vondrousova and the DCO gave differing accounts as to what happened next, with the former suggesting that they had one more exchange via intercom, and the latter two.

10 minutes after their conversation, Vondrousova left her building to find the DCO still waiting to administer the test as she took her Italian greyhound for a walk.

Vondrousova was then prompted a final time by the DCO that her refusal to take a test would have serious consequences, and signed a form which confirmed her decision before continuing on her dog walk.

'She left,' Vondrousova messaged Molina, before sending him a picture of her completed form. '(T)his is completely f***ed up.' She later posted a statement about the incident, including a picture of the DCO and tagging the ITIA and World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) on her Instagram Story.

Both Vondrousova and Molina claimed to have no knowledge that players could be tested outside of their specified window.

All players in the ITIA testing pool must share a time and location where they are available for testing every day, updating it as necessary, with Vondrousova's scheduled for the morning.

But the organisation consistently stressed that out-of-competition and out-of-hours testing is imperative to ensure clean sport, with the ITIA regularly sharing information on their 'any time, any place' guidelines - which was cited during the tribunal.

Molina had spoken to the organisation that evening at around 9pm, sharing that he had never had a client tested outside of their window and querying whether it was a 'new' initiative.

The ITIA argued that Vondrousova, who has taken 83 tests over the last eight years, could not 'credibly' say that she was not aware of the rules.

After the incident, Vondrousova briefly shared her first account of refusing the test on her Instagram Story

While Vondrousova was deemed to have been aware that she was dealing with a DCO despite her claim that she had not identified her properly, allegations that she had been unsafe were also unpicked.

Vondrousova had cited the horrifying 2016 incident which saw her compatriot Petra Kvitova stabbed after a man pretending to be boiler repairman assaulted her at her home in Prostejov as her reasoning for why she had felt unsafe.

But despite Vondrousova's argument that her apartment was in an area of Prague with high crime rates, the tribunal disagreed, citing that the city was consistently ranked one of the safest in Europe.

Vondrousova had simultaneously admitted that she lived in a 'nice area', and the tribunal found her to have 'exaggerated' similarities to Kvitova's ordeal.

The tribunal also saw her account of feeling unsafe as being at odds with her decision to take her dog for a walk and come face-to-face with the DCO, with Vondrousova describing the small dog as 'not much of a scary dog'.

The player's claim that her 'acute stress reaction' had hampered her decision-making also faltered as neither of the two doctors who had given evidence on Vondrousova's mental wellbeing made themselves available for cross examination.

The ITIA admitted to understanding that the situation would cause some anxiety, but rejected that she had not been able to maintain a high level of cognitive function throughout the incident.

The organisation's own expert added that 'the retrospective nature of the diagnoses made by the experts which the Player relied upon (and their lack of any contemporaneous evidence to support them) presented inherent clinical risks which needed to be treated with caution'.

Vondrousova has the right to appeal the decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), but her sanction began on 22 June of this year, and if served in totality, will see her return to the WTA tour at the age of 30.

Sports.title: England refuse to rule out Ben Stokes retirement U-turn ahead of next summer's Ashes: 'Anything is possible'
Sports.content:
Rob Key has refused to rule out an Ashes return for Ben Stokes next summer, claiming: ‘Anything is possible.’

It was typical of Stokes’ show-stealing ability that on the morning that England director of cricket Key was at Lord’s explaining his decision to reappoint Joe Root as Test captain under new coach Stephen Fleming that a sensational international retirement u-turn was being floated.

Since calling time on his international career at the end of June, Stokes has slipped back into life with Durham and been the subject of an approach by Sydney Sixers to play in Australia’s Big Bash League.

Suspicion remains down under, however, that despite Stokes insisting he will be watching England v Australia matches from hospitality boxes next summer, he will at the age of 36 be back for one last hurrah against the old enemy. Even Australia coach Andrew McDonald spoke of the ‘fairytale’ of ‘one more Ashes’ earlier this week.

Asked if there had been a change of heart, Key said: ‘It would be a brilliant story if he does. He hasn't, but I wouldn't be surprised. Anything is possible with Ben.’

It will potentially be a future conversation for Fleming, whose first involvement with England will be in selection for the first Test against Pakistan on August 19, but whose work on the ground here will not commence until the following month.

Ben Stokes could reverse his decision to retire from international cricket ahead of the Ashes

England's director of cricket Rob Key has stressed that 'anything is possible' for the ex-captain

Identified by England director of cricket Rob Key as the man to haul the Test team out of its current malaise, Fleming was appointed in the knowledge that pre-existing family commitments prevented him from being in place immediately, meaning his first direct involvement will not be for several weeks.

A firm arrival date is yet to be confirmed, but it will coincide with the third Test at Edgbaston between September 9-13 at the earliest. If his first Test in charge is in South Africa next winter, he will have only one on home soil - against Bangladesh next May - ahead of Australia’s arrival.

‘My job, I believe, is to get the best person to do the job. And it wasn't a stipulation for any of the candidates that you had to be there for Pakistan. Had that been the case, that would have limited the field drastically,’ Key said.

‘It was about trying to get the best person to do that. A month ago, this was probably not on a lot of people's radar, certainly myself, Stephen Fleming, as well. In life, you have a lot of things that you have to do that have been planned a long way in advance.’

Fleming, 53, has never coached in first-class cricket before, having spent 18 months with Chennai Super Kings, and their spin-off franchises in South Africa and the United States, in addition to two seasons with Southern Brave in the Hundred.

‘He has worked with the best players in the world. We’ve seen he's up to speed with where the game's at. You don't lose that experience that you have in Test cricket, that you gain as a player, and, more importantly, as a captain,’ argued Key.

‘I've never met anyone who said a bad word about his leadership in Test cricket. I think all of those things put into the mix. I'm as optimistic as ever, really, that we've got the best people to take English cricket forward.’

Key also dismissed any notion that after four years of Fleming’s fellow New Zealander Brendon McCullum in charge, this was a juncture for an English coach to be appointed, saying: ‘I think it’s preferable to have the best coach.’

Adding of Fleming: ‘He knows English cricket really well. He's been close to it. He's obviously played in it. He has a huge amount of love and respect for the county game, in particular, what it did for him as a player, and for his development.

‘So as much as he'll be over in September, he's already sort of very much in the weeds of it all.’

Root quit the captaincy four years ago saying the job had impacted negatively on his life away from the game, particularly through the Covid period of 2020-22, but enjoyed deputising for Stokes in the second Test against New Zealand this summer and was keen to add to his England record 65 caps in charge.

‘Those two, Fleming and Root will be a great complementary pairing to take English cricket forward. He's our best ever batter. Our great cricketer, that can actually now have a chance to captain the side without any of the stuff he had to deal with last time. I'm just so glad that he gets that chance,’ Key reflected, adding that Harry Brook’s time would come further down the line.

Former New Zealand cricketer Stephen Fleming has been named Brendon McCullum's successor, with Joe Root as his captain

‘He's still developing as a player and as a person, to be honest. The Test match captaincy is the biggest job in cricket in England, and I think that it's perfect now with Joe who gets the chance to do it where he can now take this ship forward as the most senior player by a long, long way and Harry can now continue on the project he's done in the white-ball job and continue learning how to become an outstanding leader of a cricket team.

‘You've got the 2027 World Cup, all of those things, and at some stage Harry Brook will be an outstanding Test captain of England cricket. I just didn't feel the time was right now.’

Whether Key will still be around to make the appointment remains to be seen, having survived a post-Ashes review in January.

So, after losing 4-1 to Australia, did he feel lucky to keep his job? Did he fear the sack? Consider his own position?

‘I think all of the above. This is a job where you're constantly under pressure all the time. There's uncertainty in it all the time. That's part of being in this role. How close I came (to being sacked), I don't know. How close I came myself, what I was thinking, I obviously know. But it's been a good few months – and even before that – where you're constantly thinking: are you the right person? What is the thing you’ve got to do? Are you the person to put that in place? I believe I am, but that's for the people above me to decide all the time.’

Sports.title: 'Clicky Ponting' is just the tip of the iceberg. I've played club cricket for decades and these are the wildest stories of cheating, from vaseline to elastic bands and fattening up umpires to a trail of sawdust
Sports.content:
'Clicky Ponting' is just the tip of the iceberg. I've played club cricket for decades and these are the wildest stories of cheating, from vaseline to elastic bands and fattening up umpires to a trail of sawdust

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

At the snap of a finger, Brian Devine became English cricket's Public Enemy No 1 - and 'Clicky Ponting' was born.

An investigation is underway in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League after several videos appeared to show Saltburn CC slip fielder Devine clicking his fingers as the ball passed the batsman to mimic the sound of an edge.

Devine’s aim is as clear as it is shocking – to con the umpire into giving his team a wicket. The spirit of cricket this most definitely is not, and Devine and his team’s actions have shocked the cricketing world (and his now former sponsor, the local curry house).

But Saltburn are hardly the only team over the years to bend the rules – and in some cases, openly break them.

The 2018 scandal which saw three Australian cricketers receive long bans for their part in a sandpaper ball tampering plot and Alex Carey’s controversial 2023 Ashes run out of Jonny Bairstow are high-profile recent examples in international cricket.

And similar incidents to Saltburn’s have taken place regularly at grassroots level, too. We've gathered together the best (or worst, depending on your view) from decades' worth of experience in the glory, and shame, of club cricket.

Brian Devine, the man at the centre of the 'Clicky Ponting' club cricket scandal

Devine (circled) is being investigated by his local league, with allegations he clicked his fingers when the ball passed an opposition player's bat to simulate the sound of an edge

Vaseline assistance

Sunny Agnihotri played for West Blatchington Cricket Club between 2002 and 2008, and won the Sussex Invitation League Division 1 twice.

When they met Crawley Eagles, the opposition would put Vaseline on their bats ahead of the match. The idea was that when the ball nicked the outside edge, it wouldn’t make so much noise.

‘We asked the umpires about it and they said it’s not against the rules,' said Agnihotri. 'They were also definitely rummaging in their pockets between balls, so we knew something untoward was going on. They made it so obvious. The dark arts happen a lot.’

Local rivals Brighton Insurance would waste time when they batted first to use up the daylight.

Between a dismissed batsman walking off and a new one replacing him, you had three minutes. But on the field of play, you could still get padded up. Brighton players would throw all their equipment on the pitch and take longer than three minutes without punishment.

‘They would take double the time so that when it was our turn to bat, it would be gloomier,’ Agnihotri said.

Izzy Martin

But similar incidents to Saltburn’s have taken place regularly at grassroots level too

It’s not always the players…

There was an umpire in the Leicestershire leagues during the late 1990s renowned for getting a twitchy trigger finger the closer it got to opening time at the bar.

When he started to get really thirsty, he would whisper under his breath: ‘Next one that hits the pads… give it a big appeal’ and, when the fielding side did, he duly obliged.

A trick of one former Leicestershire Premier Division champion team was to send beers to the umpires' room and offer them sweets while in the field in a bid to get them on-side so decisions would fall in their favour.

‘Where there’s a will, there’s a way,’ said one member of the side. Their wicketkeeper was also known for trying to kick the stumps down and appealing that the batter had been bowled.

I remember playing in a county age-group match in which one fielder on the team, who went on to become a professional, took a catch on the half-volley and celebrated as though it was clean.

Another team in the Leicestershire leagues was once accused of sending the same batsman in twice in different kit, until their plan was foiled when the star man was spotted by the home team scorer through her binoculars.

Anonymous

No matter the spread of the 'spirit of cricket', the laws are always open to a little bending

Let's all band together

I played in a match many, many years ago where three of our batsmen were given out caught behind, all of them swearing blind they never got a nick on the ball.

After some brief research, we realised the wicketkeeper had an elastic band attached to his glove, which he snapped against it to make the noise of a nick, fooling the umpire into giving it out in a similar trick to Saltburn's.

Anonymous

Saltburn CC, which has now come under international scrutiny after Devine was caught on camera

Questionable declaration

In 2017, Pembrokeshire rivals Carew and Cresselly took on each other in the final game of that year’s West Wales league season. Carew were top, Cresselly second.

Cresselly faced a difficult task that day, but not an impossible one. Carew’s lead was 21 points and a win was worth 20, but then you had the bonuses to consider – a point for every 40 runs up to 200 and a point for every two wickets.

In short, it boiled down to this: if Cresselly could win and take two more bonus points than Carew, they’d snatch the title. But Carew had a devilish plan.

As far as I’ve been told in my retracing of the steps, they even checked the rules with the umpire before the game, found their read of the situation was accurate, and set about putting it in action.

Batting first, they declared on just 18 for one. First there was shock, then revulsion. It was filthy and entirely legal.

Cresselly were welcome to the 20 points, which they achieved by knocking off the chase in just a few overs, but the opportunity for any bonuses had been snatched clean off the table. It was Carew’s title by a single point.

Riath Al-Samarrai

Saltburn weren't the first side to mimick an edge - one of our contributors played against a team whose wicketkeeper used an elastic band!

Bailout

One day, while in action for Saffron Plantationers – a village side in Quendon near Saffron Walden in Essex – I was at the crease with my team needing four runs to win.

My plan was to charge the bowler and hit the ball down the ground. I was still deep in my crease as the bowler ran in. But his delivery was short of a length, so I stepped back and pulled it for four. As I did so, however, I trod gently on my own stumps and off came the bails.

But instead of me being given out hit wicket, as I should have been, everyone at the ground watched the ball disappear to the boundary. Not seeing the bails were off, the umpire signalled four and the end of the game.

After a while, the opposition wicketkeeper noticed something off and questioned why the bails were no longer on the stumps. But I just kept walking off the pitch as technically, the game was now over.

It was one I got away with but I’m not proud of my actions – I got caught up in the moment and should have fessed up. I do seem to remember sleeping OK that night though!

Matt Gatward

Australia captain Steve Smith breaks down at a press conference in light of his side's Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal in 2018

Another cheat bites the dust

I remember playing for Eynsford at Chislehurst and West Kent one year in the Kent leagues.

Eynsford were interrupted in their victory charge by a short, sharp shower. After 20 minutes off the field to allow the pitch to dry, the umpires suggested a restart and asked Chislehurst to put out some sawdust for the bowlers to allow for better grip.

The response from the Chislehurst captain was: ‘Sorry, we haven’t got any.’

Unfortunately for him, a visiting member had seen him put a bag from the club shed into his car boot, leaving a trail of sawdust between the two locations. When called out, he had the front to say he knew nothing about it!

Anonymous

No age allowances

Not cheating as such, though by way of intimidation it comes close to the line.

I distinctly remember my senior debut in the adult leagues. As someone who had a modicum of talent and was playing Northamptonshire junior cricket at the time, I was chucked in alongside grown men aged just 13 in a bid to speed up my development.

Cricket is meant to be a sport played by gentlemen - but don't be surprised if you hear a few expletives at a village game, no matter how young the person on the receiving end is

Playing for South Northamptonshire village side Marston St Lawrence, I faced a tough task against experienced cricketers. Unsurprisingly given my youth, I struggled with the bat, playing and missing repeatedly.

I was as frustrated as anyone on the field, but my tender years didn’t stop me getting both barrels from the bowler who I couldn’t lay a bat on. I’ll never forget his words.

‘Just hit it, you c***!’ he shouted at me, his words starting off an unpleasant exchange with my more senior partner at the other end.

I was so shocked to be verbally abused at that age, I could not muster a reply. However, in the years since I've thought regularly about what I should have said.

If I had my time again, the response would have been: ‘I’m f***ing trying!’

Alex Bywater

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino issues new statement as feelings clear after failed World Cup plans
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino issues new statement as feelings clear after failed World Cup plans

Gianni Infantino's grand plans for the World Cup lay in tatters

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino has been forced into a humiliating climbdown (Image: Bradley Collyer/PA Wire)

Gianni Infantino issued a shameless statement just hours after his plans to sell off the World Cup were embarrassingly ripped to shreds. The controversial FIFA boss had proposed to create FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) to manage its competitions, including the World Cup.

‌



The most contentious aspect of the plan was the intention to sell a 20 per cent stake to private investors. Thrive Eternal, a company founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, had been earmarked as the lead investor. The plan was met with outcry across the football world, especially in Europe, with all 55 UEFA member associations vowing to boycott the World Cup.

‌



The Asian Confederation and CONCACAF (the association of North America and the Caribbean) also denounced Infantino's scheme. With his plot - and possibly his hold on the FIFA presidency - crumbling around him, Infantino took the time to issue a tin-eared statement highlighting the success and "unity" of the recent World Cup.

‌



On Saturday morning, the Swiss administrator took to Instagram to post: "The FIFA World Cup 2026 brought together more people, more cultures and more communities than ever before, showing the true power of the beautiful game.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"Football speaks every language and belongs to everyone. That is why I have always believed it has a unique ability to bring people together, inspire hope and create opportunities. Thank you to every fan for making this the greatest and most inclusive @fifaworldcup ever."

‌



The post included a picture of him shaking hands with a fan and ended with the hashtag #FootballUnitesTheWorld. The post attracted a few thousand likes but no comments, as they had been disabled.

Following such a stinging response to his plan, including from some of his own colleagues, Infantino has been forced into a humiliating climbdown.

In a separate statement released on Saturday, Infantino said: "The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

‌



View 2 Images Gianni Infantino has taken every opportunity to cosy up to Donald Trump (Image: Photo by Eric Verhoeven/Soccrates/Getty Images)

"And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

"Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

‌



"Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support."

With his power base severely weakened, Infantino, who is up for re-election next year, could now face a strong leadership challenge.

Sports.title: Football fans' power still strong as Gianni Infantino's World Cup plot follows Super League to scrap heap
Sports.content:
Football fans' power still strong as Gianni Infantino's World Cup plot follows Super League to scrap heap

Football fans have long been led to believe that they are losing control of the game they fell in love with but after Gianni Infantino’s dramatic U-turn, they have been shown that they can still make an impact

View 4 Images Gianni Infantino has been forced to perform an embarrassing u-turn on his plans for the World Cup (Image: Getty Images)

FIFA’s embarrassing plan to sell the World Cup lasted less than four days before it was scrapped. Under-fire president Gianni Infantino, whose position now appears to be untenable, only unveiled the woeful plot on Thursday.

‌



The reaction was instant. Football didn’t want this. And through the combined power of football supporters, governing federations and even some of Infantino’s closest advisors, the plan has landed on the scrap heap.

‌



In an effort to potentially save face, the FIFA president released a statement in the early hours of Saturday morning confirming that the plan had been cancelled entirely.

‌



It read: “The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

“And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

‌



“Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

“Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”

And while Infantino will attempt to hide his humiliating u-turn, football fans should celebrate that their strength has seen the idea binned. They were of course helped by threats of boycotts from UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation - as well as Infantino’s senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro resigning from his position.

‌



View 4 Images Gianni Infantino's position as FIFA president is surely untenable (Image: Getty Images)

It left the 56-year-old in a near-impossible position as revealed by UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister. Speaking after the news, she said: "He had to be pushed into that corner and that is regrettable of course, but I think it showed the unity of football when we face such an existential crisis.

"But it really shouldn't have come to this, I think most of us believe this was a hugely misguided and potentially catastrophic proposal and it should never have been put on the table. I am delighted we were able to fight it off."

‌



It is of course not the first time that the sheer power of fans has forced football governance to alter its course - the most infamous example being the plot behind the European Super League back in 2021.

The scandalous project was officially confirmed on April 18, with 20 of Europe’s biggest clubs confirmed to be part of it. The backlash was again instant.

View 4 Images Chelsea supporters protested against the European Super League plot (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Fans mobilised with protests outside of their club’s stadiums, the UK Government expressed its displeasure over the plans and ironically Infantino publicised his opposition. Players also spoke out, while high-profile managers including Arsene Wenger, Jurgen Klopp and Sir Alex Ferguson slammed the plot.

UEFA and FIFA (again, ironically) tried to intervene but the organisers of the Super League hit back with threats of legal proceedings in European courts designed to block any sanctions that they might have in mind.

Under the crippling weight of the fan and governing body backlash, the first cracks in the Super League plot began to show. Just 56 hours after the initial announcement, Manchester City became the first club to pull out and they were eventually followed by all of their Premier League rivals.

‌



And just like that, the European Super League was dead in just a matter of days - allowing for a couple of rogue clubs who were bizarrely willing to pursue the plans for years - but that’s another story.

View 4 Images Man City were the first Premier League side to back out of the Super League plan (Image: Getty Images)

It’s now taken less than a week for Infantino’s baffling plot to be unpicked. Football has come together to decide its future for itself.

‌



In an age where the game seems to be moving away from the common man and closer to the elite - as evidenced by the sky-high prices of this summer's World Cup - it’s heartening to know that there is still the potential for the normal, match-going supporter to have an impact on the future of the beautiful game.

It leaves Infantino in an untenable position. His intentions are now clear. While he has been able to stomach a humiliating defeat, whether he is now able to relinquish his power right at the top of FIFA remains to be seen.

Should football fans want him gone, he needs to make sure that he doesn’t underestimate their opinions. After all, he too could end up lasting days.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi's World Cup final behaviour sparks petition to strip him of prestigious award
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi's World Cup final behaviour sparks petition to strip him of prestigious award

A prestigious honour recently awarded to Lionel Messi is facing calls to be withdrawn following a furious backlash sparked by the aftermath of the 2026 World Cup final

View 3 Images Lionel Messi could have is award stripped (Image: AFP or licensors)

Calls for Lionel Messi to be stripped of the Princess of Asturias Award for Sports have intensified in the wake of the 2026 World Cup final. The prestigious honour - presented to individuals and organisations for outstanding contributions to sport, science, the humanities and public affairs - was awarded to the Argentine icon in June.

‌



In explaining its decision, the jury pointed not only to Messi's extraordinary achievements on the pitch but also praised his extensive charitable work, his exemplary on-field conduct and his perseverance, humility and commitment to team play.

‌



But that decision has since come under intense scrutiny following Argentina's 1-0 defeat to Spain in last month's World Cup final. Tempers flared at the final whistle as several Argentine players became embroiled in heated confrontations with their Spanish counterparts.

‌



Although Messi did not take part in any of the physical clashes, he and his team-mates drew criticism by turning their backs and refusing to watch Spain's trophy presentation - a gesture widely condemned as lacking in sportsmanship.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Lionel Messi's gesture to Argentina squad leaked after World Cup dressing room theories READ MORE :

The backlash has prompted multiple petitions calling for Messi to be stripped of the Princess of Asturias Award, with critics arguing his actions fell short of the standards of conduct the honour is intended to recognise.

‌



One petition argues that Messi displayed behaviour that was "unsportsmanlike and contrary to the values of respect and fair play that the sport promotes." It also states that stripping him of the award would "send a clear message about the importance of maintaining exemplary conduct in all facets of life, especially in the realm of sports."

Another initiative maintains that revoking the honour would help "restore confidence in the fairness and rigour" of these awards, which have been awarded to the likes of Al Gore, David Attenborough, Rafael Nadal and Stephen Hawking.

View 3 Images Messi finished runner-up in the World Cup for the second time in his career (Image: PATRICIA DE MELO MOREIRA / AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Messi, 39, is due to receive the award at a ceremony in October. When announcing him as the recipient, the Princess of Asturias Foundation said: "In addition to [Messi's] dazzling talent, the Jury has highlighted his exceptional sporting career and his formidable and continued charitable work to promote access to education and health care for the most disadvantaged children.

"Leo Messi, the player who has won the most titles in the history of football, has also earned the respect and admiration of everyone for his exemplary behaviour on the field and for his consistency, humility and commitment to the team game."

Messi was denied the fairy-tale ending to his international career as Argentina fell to a 1-0 extra-time defeat against Spain in the World Cup final in New Jersey. Ferran Torres struck the decisive goal shortly after Enzo Fernandez had been sent off, bringing Argentina's title defence to a heartbreaking conclusion.

‌



View 3 Images The Argentina players all stood with their backs to Spain as the winners received their World Cup medals (Image: Maja Hitij - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

Spain were worthy winners, dominating proceedings from start to finish. They enjoyed 68 per cent possession and fired 20 shots at goal, while Argentina managed just three attempts - all of them coming only after falling behind in extra time.

The match, however, was ultimately overshadowed by chaotic scenes after the final whistle. Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes is among several individuals under investigation by FIFA after being charged with three counts of violent conduct. The midfielder was seen physically manhandling two Spain players during the post-match confrontations.

Sports.title: Leandro Paredes facing minimum nine-game ban – but could avoid FIFA's Argentina punishment
Sports.content:
Leandro Paredes facing minimum nine-game ban – but could avoid FIFA's Argentina punishment

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes is facing a nine-game ban for violent conduct in the aftermath of the World Cup final - but could avoid punishment altogether after a surprise admission

View 2 Images Leandro Paredes could get off scot-free (Image: Image Photo Agency, Getty Images)

Leandro Paredes could avoid serving any suspension despite facing multiple FIFA disciplinary charges following Argentina's explosive World Cup final defeat to Spain. The Boca Juniors midfielder is under investigation for three separate counts of violent conduct after tempers erupted in the aftermath of last month's showpiece.

‌



While the charges leave him facing the prospect of a lengthy international ban, comments made after the final have opened up the possibility of an unexpected escape route. The incidents involving Paredes unfolded after the final whistle, with the Argentina international repeatedly confronting Spain players as emotions spilt over.

‌



TV footage appeared to show him kick and shove Eric Garcia before jabbing the defender in the throat. Moments later, he allegedly targeted Gavi, grabbing the midfielder before throwing him to the ground during another heated exchange.

‌



Article 14 of the FIFA Disciplinary Code states that every individual act of aggression carries a minimum three-match suspension. If Paredes is found guilty on all three charges, he could therefore receive a ban totalling nine matches.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

FIFA open disciplinary proceedings after Argentina's Falklands banner vs England READ MORE :

FIFA come down hard on Argentina stars as charges handed out after World Cup final brawl READ MORE :

However, the 32-year-old recently hinted that he could retire from international football, potentially allowing him to sidestep any immediate punishment.

‌



When asked about his future with the national team a few days after the final, Paredes replied: "I don't know. It's a process: you have to digest it, think it through, avoid making rushed decisions, and it's certainly something that needs to be discussed."

Although international retirement would initially help Paredes circumvent a prospective punishment for violent conduct, FIFA can invoke Article 70 to extend the sanction worldwide - as it did when Luis Suarez was banned from all football-related activities for four months after biting Giorgio Chiellini at the 2014 World Cup.

That type of intervention is generally reserved for the game's most severe disciplinary offences, meaning Paredes is unlikely to fall into the same category.

‌



View 2 Images Paredes (centre) has been charged with three counts of assault by FIFA

FIFA has not yet delivered its final ruling and, although a nine-match suspension remains possible under the disciplinary regulations and previous precedents, a ban of five or six games is widely viewed as the more probable outcome.

Paredes is not the only Argentina figure facing disciplinary action. Nahuel Molina has also been charged with two acts of aggression following the final - one completed and one attempted - while assistant coach Roberto Ayala is the subject of a separate aggression charge that could likewise result in a suspension.

‌



FIFA has also launched proceedings against the Argentine Football Association (AFA) over alleged discriminatory chants and gestures, breaches of match and security regulations, delays to kick-off, inappropriate messages displayed by players and supporters, and the throwing of objects.

Should those allegations be upheld, the AFA could receive a significant financial punishment and, in the most serious circumstances, face partial or complete stadium closures for future home fixtures.

Sports.title: Arsenal star refused to go on pre-season tour to force through summer transfer
Sports.content:
Arsenal star refused to go on pre-season tour to force through summer transfer

One player's actions left a bitter taste in the mouth ahead of Arsenal's pre-season tour

View 2 Images Laurent Koscielny left Arsenal just a few weeks after the 2019 Europa League final (Image: Michael Regan, Getty Images)

Former Arsenal captain Laurent Koscielny once refused to join the club’s pre-season tour in order to force through a summer transfer. Mikel Arteta’s Gunners are currently deep into their pre-season preparations.

‌



They will look to shake off any rust built up during the post-season break by taking on Girona in Spain on Saturday, August 1). The Premier League champions will then face Real Betis, Borussia Dortmund and Como in the coming days, before playing Manchester City in the Community Shield on August 16.

‌



A good pre-season plays a crucial role in providing the baseline for fitness and tactical ideas going into the new 2026/27 campaign. As such, it is hard to imagine any player within Arteta’s squad seeking to disrupt this current team’s rhythm by not flying out with the rest of the camp.

‌



FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Vinicius Jr moves step closer to Arsenal transfer after Real Madrid make contract decision READ MORE :

Bruno Guimaraes' agent teases Arsenal with Vinicius Jr post amid agreement claims READ MORE :

But things were very different in N5 before the Spaniard took over, with Arsenal going through a period of uncertainty and chaos on and off the field between 2018 and 2019, after Arsene Wenger left the club.

That was no more evident than when, during Unai Emery’s brief reign in charge, Gunners skipper Koscielny went on strike in an effort to seal a return to France. The then-33-year-old stunned the club hierarchy by informing them he was refusing to take part in the pre-season tour of America.

‌



Emery reacted furiously and immediately informed Arsenal’s then-head of football Raul Sanllehi, who sanctioned the decision to publish a statement condemning Koscielny’s actions.

The statement read: "Laurent Koscielny has refused to travel to the US for our pre-season tour. We are very disappointed by Laurent’s actions, which are against our clear instructions.

"We hope to resolve this matter and will not be providing any further comment at this time."

‌



The rest of the Arsenal squad flew to the United States without their long-serving centre-half, who instead trained with the Under-23s while a resolution was sought. Koscielny had 12 months left on his deal and felt the club were pricing him out of a departure by demanding £10m for the player.

View 2 Images Laurent Koscielny ended up joining Bordeaux in 2019 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

He was also said to have been frustrated at his playing schedule being mismanaged following the injury he suffered during the 2018 Europa League semi-final second leg against Atletico Madrid, and was dismayed at the direction in which the club was headed.

‌



The Frenchman finally got his wish on August 6, 2019, as Arsenal accepted a £4.6m offer from Bordeaux, ending the defensive veteran’s nine-year stint in north London. In his controversial transfer announcement video, Koscielny was shown ripping off an Arsenal shirt to reveal the colours of his new team - a gesture that angered fans.

The move was a huge blow for Emery on the eve of the new season, with Arsenal’s short-staffing at the back already an issue. But it removed a significant problem as Koscielny had made it clear that summer he wanted to leave.

The defender left the Emirates Stadium after making 353 appearances and winning three FA Cup trophies. He spent three seasons playing in Ligue 1 for Bordeaux.

Article continues below

After that ill-fated spell, Koscielny initially rejoined Lorient as a youth coach. He became part of the upper management when Les Merlus [the Hakes] were relegated in 2024. The club would go straight back up as champions.

Now 40, he has held the position of sporting director at the club since June 2024.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino's statement in full as FIFA's controversial World Cup plan SCRAPPED
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino's statement in full as FIFA's controversial World Cup plan SCRAPPED

Gianni Infantino has performed a rapid U-turn on his plans to sell off a share of the World Cup to foreign investors and has now explained why the plot has been binned

View 2 Images FIFA president Gianni Infantino has been forced to perform a dramatic U-turn (Image: Getty Images)

Under-fire FIFA president Gianni Infantino has explained that 'division' within football was a driving force behind the decision to scrap his World Cup sale plan. World football’s governing body unveiled the plot to auction off a share in the tournament to private investment groups earlier this week.

The plan was met with huge backlash from across the footballing landscape, with UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC all against the plan. Many had threatened to boycott upcoming FIFA tournaments in protest.

Meanwhile, one of Infantino’s closest advisors Carlos Cordeiro, as well as FIFA Chief Operating Officer Kevin Lamour, spoke out in opposition, with the former resigning from his post.

But the plan has now been binned entirely. A statement from FIFA President Infantino in the early hours of Saturday morning read: “The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

“And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

Article continues below

“Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

“Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino consulted Donald Trump's administration about his plan (Image: Getty Images)

There has already been praise for Infantino’s u-turn. Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Shaikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa said: "The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game.

“The AFC stands ready to support any initiative that strengthens the unity of the football family, contributes to the continued growth of the game globally and delivers meaningful benefits to all stakeholders.”

He added: “I am proud that all our MAs stood together and entrusted the AFC to seek answers on their behalf regarding an issue of immense importance to the future governance of world football. I thank them for their patience, solidarity and unity, and assure them that AFC will always act in their best interests.”

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
