World.title: Dreaming of representing Canada at Eurovision? These Canadian former contestants have some advice
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Eurovision is basically the Olympics of the song contest world, and 2027 will be the first time Canada competes on the world stage in front of millions of spectators.

It's still too soon to say how Canada's act will be chosen, but as any athlete will tell you, it's never too soon to start preparing for the international media, the next-level fans or winning over voters.

CBC News tracked down four of the nine Canadians who have performed in previous Eurovision Song Contests, and asked what kind of advice they would give to future Canadian contestants.

Passionate fans

More than 130 million people watched the most recent Eurovision Song Contest, and it has another four million followers on TikTok.

Eurovision superfans dedicate countless hours watching past contests and familiarizing themselves with the songs and biographical details of their favourite performers. They host discord channels and radio shows, attend watch parties and some even dress up to pay tribute to beloved acts.

Decades after Quebecer Annie Cotton's third-place finish on behalf of Switzerland in 1993, fans still reach out to her to ask for autographed photos, or just to let her know how much they loved her performance.

Quebecer Annie Cotton represented Switzerland at Eurovision in 1993. (Jean-Charles Labarre)

But it took a while for Cotton to realize how devoted Eurovision fans can be. Canadians didn’t know much about the contest when she performed in 1993, because it wasn't broadcast in Canada and most people still didn't have the internet.

"I didn't know how much this show was reaching fans,” she said of that era. "But when the internet arrived in our lives, then I realized that many countries have websites on Eurovision history and participants."

International promotion

Vancouver-born Rykka, who performed on behalf of Switzerland in 2016, understands that fan appreciation. "I really love the Eurovision community, they're amazing, like the fans and everybody. Very, very warm and a lot of fun," she said.

For Rykka, the workload that came with participating in Eurovision was also overwhelming. "It was definitely like a whole half a year project," she said.

First, there was a selection process for Switzerland to choose its submission, which included a television show and national voting. Then there was an intensive planning phase followed by showcases in several different countries — all before the actual contest got underway.

"I'm very grateful and I had a lot of amazing, super unique experiences. But also it took a lot of energy in special ways that I had to recover from for a long time," Rykka said.

Vancouver-born performer Rykka represented Switzerland at Eurovision in 2016, says the contest took a lot of her energy. (Lynol Lui)

Gary Lux, who was born in Peterborough, Ont., has been part of six different Eurovision contests. The first time was in 1983 when he performed as part of the Austrian pop group Westend.

He too admits " promotion is not easy." But he said it is important to be disciplined and push through because "when you feel that the success comes, that pushes the energy incredibly."

All those showcases and media performances are an essential part of winning over the voters who will have a role in picking the Eurovision winner.

Representing Canada

Whoever is going to Bulgaria in 2027 will have another important role: representing Canada to global allies. That's a lot of press ure — especially during what will be Canada's first appearance.

"I think that the Canadians have a good standing in the minds of the Europeans," said Lux.

Gary Lux was born in Peterborough, Ont., and performed at Eurovision on behalf of Austria on six different occasions. (Martin Hauser/Catchlight)

But there ar e still ways to ingratiate a performer with the crew and audience in the host country, who can help bolster a performance.

"I would suggest reading up about the country, maybe learning a couple of words in Bulgarian, finding out as much as you can before you get there," said Sherisse Laurence, from Huntsville, Ont. That's what she did before she went to Norway for Eurovision on behalf of Luxembourg in 1986.

"In rehearsal spaces I would start playing some [Norwegian composer Edvard] Grieg and that would really warm up the Norwegian crew towards me."

How to win

Eurovision fans may love an over-the-top performance, but these former contestants feel that is a trap Canada shouldn’t fall into at its first Eurovision Song Contest.

"The most important thing is to be authentic," said Lux. "What the people really [want is] if you catch them emotionally. Then everything can happen."

That worked for Cotton in Ireland in 1993.

" I remember I sang a song called Moi, tout simplement [I will be myself]," she said. "I was 17 years old, in the middle of the huge stage, alone by myself, with no dancers, no backing vocalists, just me.… People liked it."

Sherisse Laurence, left, represented Luxembourg at the Eurovision Song Contest in 1986. She now works as a musician and theatre performer in Huntsville, Ont., and the surrounding area. (Sandy Raven)

Laurence's advice is, avoid anything that voters can interpret as diva-like behaviour.

"Whoever represents the country… part of the task is to convince people that, 'Hey, we belong here and we're really happy to be here.' That's the thing. Show appreciation that you are there."

Career expectations

Despite the exposure Eurovision provides, there's no guarantee a great performance will transform into a dream job.

Lux said Eurovision marked the beginning of his musical career. "When you represent your country, you're in the newspapers, the people see your picture, they see what you're about."

But Cotton doesn't feel all that exposure had a big effect. "I was working there in Switzerland and everything was going very, very fast. I was very far from home, away from my friends, my parents."

She was 17 and says she felt alone after the Eurovision Song Contest was over. "So I decided to come back because I wasn't ready for all this big thing that was happening to me."

Québecoise star Celine Dion, seen here giving a recorded message during the dress rehearsal for the final of the Eurovision Song Contest 2025, won Eurovision in 1988 on behalf of Switzerland. (Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images)

Rykka said she does not regret taking part in Eurovision, but she doesn't like her name being associated with the contest and what it stands for today.

"A lot of the venues that I was previously playing at wouldn't book me anymore because I took part in Eurovision," she said.

"It's like it was kind of like a choice between going mainstream or staying kind of like cool. But in the end I did not have mainstream benefits."

She still performs as Rykka, but right now she's focusing more on her folk duo project Goldschatz, playing smaller venues and house shows.

World.title: Canadians ready to play ball as 1st season of Women's Pro Baseball League gets underway
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nearly a dozen Canadian athletes are going to be part of the chase to be the first-ever champions of the Women's Pro Baseball League, which begins its inaugural season in the U.S. this weekend.

British Columbia's Claire Eccles will be among them, wearing a New York Heights jersey as the team takes on the Los Angeles Queens at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield, Ill., on Saturday in the WPBL's first ever game.

"I feel really lucky, I feel really honoured," said Eccles, a veteran outfielder and pitcher, who never believed she'd get the chance to play professional baseball.

But that day has come and Eccles says it's a privilege to be part of what's about to unfold.

"I'm not taking that for granted at all," said Eccles, whose Heights teammates include three fellow Canadians — Jaida Lee of St. John's, Madison Willan of Edmonton and Élodie Ciamarro of Mont-Saint-Hilaire, Que.

Newfoundland's Jaida Lee is on deck during a WPBL exhibition game in March. Lee is among the Canadians playing in the new league. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)

They're among 11 Canadians on the rosters of the WPBL's four teams, which include the Heights and the Queens, along with the Boston Hunters and the San Francisco Firebells.

Wil lan, a multi-sport athlete who played hockey and golf at the University of Alberta, told CBC's Radio Active that "it's really exciting that a lot of Canadians are getting a chance to play."

Keith Stein, the league's Canadian CEO and co-founder, is proud to see so many ballplayers from north of the border taking the field in the days and weeks ahead.

"We produce great Canadian baseball players and the women are some of the best athletes in the world," said Stein, a lawyer and entrepreneur from Toronto.

The WPBL is the only professional women's baseball league in the United States — though it is not the first. It follows in the footsteps of the famed All-American Girls Professional Baseball League, which folded in the 1950s.

Élodie Ciamarro takes batting practice in Florida in March. She's among the 11 Canadians playing in the WPBL as opening day arrives for the league's inaugural season. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)

The season ahead

After Saturday's opening day, the second game of the season will see the Firebells play the Hunters on Sunday.

After that, the league's games are scheduled to run Wednesday through Sunday, with all the action taking place at Robin Roberts Stadium, a 5,200-seat facility in Springfield.

Each WPBL team will play 15 games, prior to playoffs that will determine the league's first-ever champions in September.

Canadian fans will be able to watch WPBL games on YouTube, while ESPN and the Scripps Sports Network will air the league's regular-season and playoff games in the U.S.

Stein says it's taken a lot of work to get the league to this point, but it's also been gratifying to see the support it's received so far.

Keith Stein, the Canadian co-founder of the WPBL, chats with pitcher Ayami Sato during a practice in Fort Myers, Fla., in March. Sato was the second overall pick in the WPBL's first-ever draft. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)

Making sacrifices for the game

As of the mid-week, Stein said more than 20,000 tickets had been snapped up, and t he league had announced well before the weekend that opening day was sold out.

"It's really hard starting a new league," said Stein, who was part of the ownership group of Toronto's Arena Football League franchise, and is among the owners of the Toronto Maple Leafs baseball franchise.

The players are making sacrifices to be part of the new league: Many have day jobs and some are in school, meaning that they are having to work around those commitments in join the WPBL.

Eccles, for instance, has a full time job with Canada Soccer and she's appreciative that her employer is allowing her to arrange her work so she can play.

Media reports from Forbes and the Sports Business Journal have said each WPBL team has a budget of $95,000 US to cover player salaries.

WPBL tryouts were held at Nationals Park in Washington, D.C., last summer, and more than 600 ballplayers participated.

"I was just so blown away," said Stein, who noted that the players travelled at their own expense, for their shot at a chance to play pro ball.

A draft followed in the fall, which saw 120 players selected. But getting drafted was not a guarantee of getting a contract, so roughly half the draftees are on rosters for opening day.

Hats featuring the logos of the four WPBL teams are seen on display at the New Era Flagship Store in New York City in July. (Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

Hunger for a championship

Alongside the Canadians and many Americans playing in the WPBL, the league also counts players from Mexico, Curaçao, Japan, South Korea and Australia.

Closer to home, the Fruitvale, B.C.,-born Alli Schroder is another Canadian getting ready for her moment in the pros — and looking to see how far her team, the Boston Hunters, can go.

"I'm really excited and hoping to take on a leadership role on the team and bring a championship home to Boston in the first year of this league," the right-handed pitcher told CBC's Radio West, ahead of the start of the season.

Fellow Canadians Raine Padgham, who hails from Abbotsford, B.C., and Maïka Dumais of Quebec City — both of whom are also pitchers — will be representing Boston alongside Schroder.

Canadian ballplayer Alli Schroder is seen pitching during a tryout for the Women's Pro Baseball League at Nationals Park in Washington, D.C., last summer. The WPBL's first-ever season gets underway on Saturday, Aug. 1, and Schroder is a member of the league's Boston Hunters. (Jess Rapfogel/Getty Images)

The Los Angeles Queens have just a single Canadian on their roster: Michelle Roche, a right-handed pitcher from Burnaby, B.C.

The San Francisco Firebells, meanwhile, have three Canadians: Liz Gilder, a left-handed pitcher from Port Moody, B.C., who is a self-described "thrower of baseballs," according to her Instagram; Andréanne Leblanc, an infielder from a Montreal suburb; and Ela Day-Bédard, an infielder and university student from Gatineau, Que.

Like Eccles, the call to play pro ball was something Gilder didn't see happening for her.

"I actually didn't think that there would be women's professional baseball in my playing career," Gilder told CBC News after being drafted last November.

When draft day came and her name was called, "I felt shocked," Gilder said, adding it was also "really cool."

World.title: Kayaker on St. John River makes a pair of grim discoveries
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Melissa Lavigne has done a lot of kayaking on the St. John River in Fredericton.

But recently, as she explored the shoreline on the city's south side, she came across a couple of grave discoveries, one with a possible link to a passenger on the Mayflower.

Lavigne found a headstone and a grave marker for two different men, buried 67 years apart in different cemeteries, kilometres away from each other.

“It’s very weird,” Lavigne said. “I hope this river isn’t trying to tell me something.”

WATCH | A headstone more than 100 years old pokes out of St. John River: A pair of grave discoveries made by Fredericton kayaker | Duration 4:07 A kayaker out for a paddle discovered a headstone and a grave marker in the St. John River in Fredericton.

The headstone was visible during the summer's low water, partially submerged against the rocky shore.

Some lettering is worn away on each side, but what's visible on the stone reads:

WARD BYRON

BORN 7th APRIL

DIED 24th NOVEMBER 04.

The stone rests about 100 metres upriver from the Westmorland Street Bridge.

Other than the text, the headstone is not unlike other stones along the riverbank.

Melissa Lavigne came across the headstone while kayaking upriver from the Westmorland Street Bridge. (Shane Fowler/CBC News)

“It looked like just another rock on the side of the river,” Lavigne said.

But those few letters and dates on the stone can tell a lot.

A man buried a little more than three kilometres away shares the same name and dates.

This obituary for E. F. Byron Winslow has the same names and dates as the headstone found in the river. (Submitted by the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick)

Records from the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick list an Edward Byron Winslow as being born April 7, 1842, and dying on Nov. 24, 1904.

Winslow's obituary calls him “a prominent lawyer and citizen of Fredericton," and says he died "after a long illness of brain trouble.”

Winslow was associated with J.J. Fraser, a former lieutenant-governor of New Brunswick, the obituary says, and he was a direct descendant of “Edward Winslow, who came to America in the Mayflower in 1620.”

Despite the headstone poking out of the river, Winslow is now buried at the Forest Hill Cemetery under a headstone complete with his full name and dates for his birth and death.

Josh Green of the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick was able to track down details on the headstone and grave marker found by Lavigne in the St. John River. (Shane Fowler/CBC News)

Josh Green, manager at the provincial archives who helped track down Winslow's details, said he has no idea how the headstone wound up in the river.

But his theory is that the stone in the river may have been discarded after a spelling error or design flaw during the engraving.

The caption on a photo from the archives is worded: 'Baxter's Granite and Freestones work Queen Street west - Fredericton, ca. 1900. In the 1901 census a Smual Baxter is listed as a stone cutter. He may have been the proprietor. - [1890-1910]' (From the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick P32/32 (Item))

“There was a stonecutter at the west end of Queen Street that we found that was around in 1900, which is around the same time that this fella passed away,” Green said. “That’s rank speculation, but it did exist. Baxter's Stone Works.”

“I’ve never heard of that before,” said Kathryn Murphy, a manager at Wolastoq Adventures, a rental service for canoes and kayaks that operates about a half-kilometre away from the grave stone.

“That’s awesome, a really neat discovery.”

She said she’ll direct customers to check it out now that she knows it’s there.

Kathryn Murphy rents canoes and kayaks near where the headstone was found. (Shane Fowler/CBC News)

As for Lavigne’s second grim discovery, she said she fished a small grave marker out of the river later on her same trip.

The small silver and gold-coloured placard reads: ‘Walter F. Blair 1892-1971."

Lavigne found a grave marker for Walter Blair while kayaking. (Submitted by Melissa Lavigne)

According to New Brunswick’s vital statistics records, Blair was born at the Victoria Public Hospital, now the Victoria Health Centre, which sits by the riverbank where Lavigne found his grave marker.

According to records from the provincial archives, he was a major in the military and an accountant when he became a civilian.

“Walter Blair served with the 104th Regiment, and he served in both world wars,” Green said. “We actually have a photograph of him in his military uniform.”

In this 1937 picture are, front row, left to right, Paul Tait, Wallace Cameron, Walter Blair, York McLean, Robert Wilby and Norman Burgoine, and back row, left to right, Robert Brennan, Unknown, McKeel (first name unknown), Jerry Hanson, Joe Flannagan and Charles Fisher. (Submitted by the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick)

Blair is buried in the extension of the Fredericton Rural Cemetery just upriver from where Lavigne found the marker.

Lavigne and her husband made arrangements to have the marker returned to Blair’s surviving family members.

Stuart Blair said he was a child when Walter died, so he didn't know him personally, but he was pleased to receive the marker. He plans to give it to a Blair relative who keeps track of family history and related mementos.

Lavigne, meanwhile, is hoping future kayak trips will be less eventful.

“Well, that’s a lot of death in this river.”

World.title: What French communities have learned after a week of battling wildfires that threaten their way of life
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When he walked into his home after evacuation orders were lifted in nearly a dozen French communities hit by wildfires Thursday, Frédéric Delbreil says everything was frozen in time.

"It was strange," said Delbreil, 51, a chef at Bistrot La Nautique in Bordeaux. He lives in a small hamlet near Saint-Jean-d'Illac, a suburb of the large city in southwestern France.

Every surface inside his home was coated with grey ash, Delbreil told CBC on Friday at a volunteer hub set up in a sports complex next to a middle school.

The night before, Delbreil and his family were among the 144,000 people in France given the go-ahead to return to their homes. When he returned, he found objects in places they didn't belong — they'd been scattered in his family's rush to leave late last Friday night.

"It’s not easy to describe," he said. "You feel like smiling and crying at the same time."

WATCH | The rush to save Bordeaux: Inside France's battle to save Bordeaux from unprecedented wildfires | Duration 2:58 CBC News gets a frontline look at France's pitched fight against unprecedented wildfires in the historic Bordeaux region, where another heatwave is expected to fuel flames that have forced at least 250,000 people from their homes.

The community's homes were spared but flames brushed the edges of town as they inched closer to Bordeaux. If it weren't for firefighters and water bombing planes, Delbreil says the 20 homes on his street would be gone.

Delbreil's restaurant has been cooking food for firefighters all week in Saint-Jean-d'Illac, even as its workers are displaced. Eighty per cent of the municipality's staff had to evacuate their homes, according to Charlène Bailleul, the town's services director.

Charlène Bailleul, left, and Christelle Delbreil, two city officials in Saint-Jean-d'Illac near Bordeaux, France, discuss volunteer operations Friday. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

Bailleul and her daughter were away from their home when the order to evacuate came late last week.

Her daughter would have to cope without her plushie — and Bailleul had to spring into action to help her community. She hasn't stopped since.

On Monday, the local child-care centre will re-open, but the emergency hasn't completely ended as the ground continues to smoulder.

The bustle of the volunteer hub in Saint-Jean-d'Illac on Friday captured the transition facing communities across southwestern France as they move from crisis response to regaining some semblance of normalcy while figuring out how to live with wildfires that threaten an entire way of life.

Volunteers serve meals to firefighters on Friday in Saint-Jean-d'Illac, France, near Bordeaux. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

Reviewing lessons from a week of fires

The pine forest plantations surrounding Bordeaux that stretch to the Atlantic Ocean were planted in the 19th century in an effort to turn the area's wetlands into productive industries where growing cities could harvest the trees.

The topsoil is now dry and sandy — flooding when it rains and struggling to retain moisture in periods of drought.

Fires outside Bordeaux aren't unusual, but they're typically small and easily contained.

Last week, that changed as a wildfire in the Gironde region spread at an alarming rate that French authorities failed to predict. Bailleul says it was the first time a fire that began elsewhere travelled to their community.

"Naturally, we will need to review the lessons learned," Bailleul said, noting Saint-Jean-d'Illac itself is well prepared, with a team dedicated to forest fire prevention working year-round.

But she wants better access to national services in the future, echoing complaints from across Gironde this week when communities had to step up because the French government did not.

People filled cubic water tanks from nearby lakes and ferried them back and forth to firefighters at the scene; fed firefighters; helped with evacuations and reintegration, as well as with health care and child care.

The work has been endless, and people in the region are starting to tire.

Bordeaux-area restaurant owners and workers, from left, Frédéric Delbreil, Pascale Sirieix and Maxime Frère, have been serving meals to firefighters. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

From preparedness to prevention

But rest is not an option right now for those returning to the region.

As Delbreil says, "It's going to happen again."

That's why city councillor Caroline Esteve wants more than just preparedness, she wants prevention.

"We need to change our forestry practices, because pine trees burn extremely easily," she said.

WATCH | Returning to survey wildfire destruction in Le Porge, France: Bordeaux residents survey devastation after wildfire torches village | Duration 3:08 Residents of Le Porge in France's historic Bordeaux region show CBC News what's left of their community after a devastating wildfire tore through the village, destroying over 180 homes.

Already, the forest has been cut back several hundred metres along most roads in Gironde, in an effort to prevent flames from spreading.

Esteve says other species should be planted to alternate with pines, in addition to more market crops like carrots and potatoes — produce that can halt fire in its tracks due to high moisture content.

"It's not part of foresters' mindset yet," she said. "Pines bring in money faster."

In the parking lot by the volunteer hub, firefighters rested on patches of dry grass covered in the orange needles of the pines towering above. Many of the pines further in the Gironde area don't rise higher than a storey or two and are packed in neat rows sweeping over kilometres, but in Saint-Jean-d'Illac they're old and tall.

Katia Rigal returned to her home in Saint-Jean-d'Illac, France, near Bordeaux, after she and her family left under evacuation orders due to wildfires last week. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

Taking comfort in volunteering

At a picnic table under the conifer canopy, Katia Rigal takes a break from serving firefighters lunch with her fellow volunteers.

She, too, returned home the previous night, and like Delbreil, she says it felt weird.

Propane tanks lay underwater in their backyard pool. They were instructed to place them there by local officials after firefighters were injured by tanks that exploded in the blazes last week. Cabinets were flung open and emptied, photos were missing, taken by the family when they left in haste.

"It was a mess," said Rigal, looking away as she described the disarray of the home she returned to.

What they've been through has been difficult, but being part of the volunteer effort, keeping busy, smiling and laughing with neighbours, "it helps," she said.

"It's a pleasure to feel useful."

World.title: Canadian 4x100m relay teams advance to finals at Commonwealth Games
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian men's and women's 4x100-metre relay teams earned their way into their respective finals at the Commonwealth Games on Saturday in Glasgow.

Canada's men's team of Aaron Brown, Jerome Blake, Duan Asemota, and Andre De Grasse finished second in their heat in 38.53 seconds to advance to the final. Nigeria won the heat in 38.46, and Australia was third in 38.69 to earn automatic qualification for the final.

WATCH | Canadian men earn place in 4x100m final: Canada's men's 4x100m relay team advances to Commonwealth Games final | Duration 1:31 Canada's Aaron Brown, Jerome Blake, Duan Asemota and Andre De Grasse advanced to the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games men's 4x100-metre relay final, with a time of 38.52 seconds.

South Africa (38.30) won the second men's heat, while Ghana (38.40) and England (38.90) finished second and third, respectively. Jamaica (39.13) and Kenya (39.66) put down the next fastest times to earn the two non-automatic qualifying spots.

The Canadian women's foursome of Frédérique Chiasson, Audrey Leduc, Marie-Éloïse Leclair, and Sade McCreath won their heat in 43.15 to book their spot in the final. Trinidad and Tobago (43.31) finished second and Australia (43.52) finished third to claim the other two automatic qualification spots in the heat.

WATCH | Canadian women win their 4x100m relay heat: Canada's women's 4x100m relay team win their heat to advance to Commonwealth Games final | Duration 4:11 Canada's Frederique Chiasson, Audrey Leduc, Marie-Eloise Leclair and Sade McCreath won their heat, and finished second overall with a time of 43.15 seconds, to advance to the women's 4x100-metre relay final at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games.

The Jamaican women had the top qualifying time in the second heat, crossing the line in 42.74. Nigeria (43.93) and England (44.11) took the other two automatic spots in the final. Rounding out the lineup for the women's final are Scotland (44.89) and The Gambia (44.68).

Delgado claims boxing silver

Canadian boxer Scarlett Delgado will bring home a silver medal after a loss in the women's 54kg final on Saturday at the Commonwealth Games.

India's Preeti Pawar scored a unanimous decision victory over Delgado, of Brampton, Ont.

WATCH | Canada's Delgado takes silver in women's 54kg final: Scarlett Delgado takes silver after losing in Commonwealth Games gold medal bout | Duration 16:36 India's Preeti Pawar scored a unanimous decision victory over Scarlett Delgado of Brampton, Ont., in the women's 54kg gold medal bout at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games.

The Canadian had defeated England's Lauren Mackie 4-1 on Friday to advance to the final.

World.title: Conrad Black: Trump’s unfair tariffs are an opportunity for Canada
World.content:
Article content

Mark Carney after 16 months as prime minister, one third of the normal term and already longer than (in a few weeks) six former prime ministers, has shown no recognition of the principal requirements for increasing economic growth and narrowing the unprecedentedly large gap that has arisen between the per capita income of the United States (US$94,000) and Canada (US$60,000, behind, inter alia and with no acceptable excuse, Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, Australia, Sweden, Israel, Austria, Germany, Belgium and the United Kingdom). Even though Canada now has a lower per capita income than the United States, predictably, the Toronto Star and the Globe and Mail are waffling that a larger percentage of Canadians than Americans have an acceptable and sustainable standard of living because the United States has a larger poor underclass and a larger percentage of people of extremely great wealth. This is a quibble — the issue is that the total per capita amount of wealth in Canada has declined uncompetitively in the last decade opposite the United States, the country that for most of our history we were only narrowly behind by that measurement. How the national incomes are divided follows social and political preferences. The Americans are rugged individualists still dealing with the legacy of slavery and reckless immigration. By the universally recognized measurement of per capita national income, we are not competitive, and this government is not moving perceptibly to reverse that failure.
