World.title: PPA: Nõmme migrant case is not an isolated incident
World.content:
The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) detained 15 suspected illegal migrants on Thursday in a Tallinn suburb, but said similar incidents have occurred elsewhere. The agency asked the public to be vigilant but "reasonable," stressing "not everyone with a different skin color is problematic."

The PPA has said the migrants have likely entered the European Union after illegally crossing the Latvian-Belarus border. Politicians and the security services say the route is part of a "hybrid attack" by the Minsk authorities with Russian support.

The uptick in migrants in Estonia is likely caused by additional checks on Poland's northern and western borders to stop people smugglers traveling to Germany. The destination has now changed to Finland and Scandinavia, the PPA has said. Over 80 have been caught in the last two weeks, compared to 39 last year.

When police arrived at the scene in a suburb in the south of the capital, they initially detained 12 people. Three others had already left the area, but authorities caught them a few hours later.

Neighbors alerted the police after noticing people whose appearance and behavior stood out in the neighborhood.

The migrants were detained outside the guesthouse. The building's owner told ERR that he had not been aware of them staying at the property, although the house was later found in disarray. The owner said they had no security camera footage or other evidence confirming that the people had stayed at their accommodation.

Police operation on Tallinn's Nõmme district on Thursday. Source: Private collection

Local residents told ERR that even late in the evening, after 11 p.m., plainclothes police officers could be seen around the house. Dogs were used in the search early in the evening, and drones were also deployed. Searches were also carried out in a nearby forest.

Indrek Aru, head of the Border Guard Bureau of the North Prefecture, said on Friday that no additional people were found during the late-night searches.

"If there is reason to believe that there may be people somewhere who have no legal basis to stay in Estonia, then naturally we verify such information. That is what we did yesterday in Nõmme. When we detained a larger group of people in the area who presumably had no legal basis to stay here, we naturally looked around more broadly, and that is how those operations were carried out," he said.

However, the police are not certain that all 15 people detained on Thursday belonged to the same group.

"There is obviously reason to look for those connections, and that work is still ongoing," Aru added.

The PPA has not disclosed its communication with the property owner. However, Aru stressed that accommodation providers are obliged to verify whether third-country nationals arriving to use their services have a legal basis to stay in the country by checking their documents.

"Naturally, verifying and complying with those requirements is more complicated in the case of guest apartments offered for short-term rental," Aru acknowledged.

Fifteen suspected illegal migrants were arrested in Tallinn's Nõmme district on July 30. It is assumed they were trying to travel on to Finland. Source: Helen Wright/ OSM/ Datawrapper

He urged owners of rental properties to notify the police if a large number of people arrive at their guest apartment who may not have a legal basis to stay, or if they appear exhausted and as though they have arrived from difficult conditions.

Although the group of migrants detained in Nõmme attracted considerable attention, it was not an exceptional case for the PPA.

"We have also discovered groups of foreign nationals who presumably do not have a valid legal basis to stay at other accommodation establishments and in other districts," Aru said. "What happened in Nõmme is not an isolated case; we have had a couple of similar incidents. The Nõmme case simply attracted greater public attention this time because a significantly larger police response was involved."

Police have received unfounded reports based on skin color

Minister of Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) has also urged people to report suspicious individuals.

However, the Police have already received unfounded reports about people based solely on their skin color.

"I have heard about a few cases where people drew our attention to someone and even approached us on the street, saying they had seen someone who was probably staying in the country illegally or without a legal basis. It later turned out that the person had all the necessary documents, was completely law-abiding, and even spoke Estonian," Aru said.

"I would certainly recommend maintaining a reasonable approach," the PPA representative stressed. "Even today we are seeing well-intentioned reports, but it is important to remain reasonable when making notifications. Not everyone with a different skin color is problematic. This should be viewed in a balanced way."

A police van at the Port of Tallinn. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

The PPA is also carrying out additional checks across the country, not only Tallinn and Harju County where the main ports and airports are located.

Aru said police resources have not been exhausted.

"There is no reason for people in Estonia to worry. If you call 112, the police will come, and they do so quite quickly. Estonia has a very good emergency response time. When migration pressure increases, cooperation between countries also increases," he said.

Aru explained that this type of illegal migration is being facilitated by the authorities in Russia and Belarus.

"Naturally, people in the countries of origin of migration are looking for a better life or have other reasons for setting out. But the fact that they have chosen such a route and end up entering our visa area illegally clearly shows that this is a hybrid attack by Belarus," he said.

Migrants have been crossing the Belarusian border into Latvia, Lithuania and Poland since 2021, in what European officials say is a manufactured hybrid attack orchestrated by the Belarusian regime. The issues started after the EU sanctioned Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko.

Migrants cross the border and then try to travel onto western or northern Europe. Last year, Germany and Poland introduced checks on their borders in an attempt to stop people smugglers. Over the past year, several drivers transporting migrants have been stopped at the Polish-Lithuanian border, and now the flow has redirected northwards, the PPA said on Wednesday.

World.title: Aimar Ventsel: In Moldova, Kazakhstan and Georgia, Russia is 'one of us'
World.content:
In Estonia there is a clear distance toward Russia; for many Georgians, Kazakhs and Moldovans, by contrast, Russia occupies the same space and world, writes Aimar Ventsel.

I was recently in Georgia. To be honest, I didn't just visit — I stayed for about a month. I must say I chose the worst possible time to be in Georgia. Late June and July are the hottest period, and I often suffered in temperatures reaching 37 degrees.

I spent time in several parts of Georgia, from Adjara to Kakheti, and in some places in between. In plain language, I was in the far south near the Turkish border and then a bit in central Georgia. In April I was in Kazakhstan, mainly in the northern part, around the city of Karaganda. And a few years ago I spent several months in Moldova.

Sometimes it is useful to spend longer periods in different former Soviet republics. It gives reason to reflect on quite a few things.

As many surely know, economically and institutionally the Baltic states are the most developed among the fragments of the former Soviet Union. It is hard to say who holds the leading position; Estonians would of course like to think it is the Republic of Estonia. The same claim cannot be denied to Lithuania or Latvia.

But there is one thing in which Estonia stands out most: here the Soviet Union is the least important reference point. By that I mean that although the Soviet past is mentioned fairly often, compared with the post‑Soviet countries I have visited, it is still pleasantly rare. One could say Estonia has left the Soviet past behind and looks forward.

Georgia is a complete catastrophe in this regard. It is very hard to find anyone over forty who does not sooner or later start talking about the Soviet Union, comparing life "under the communists." And "communist" is not always a swear word in Georgia.

I have of course met people, mainly entrepreneurs, who say things are better now, that they can run their business without restrictions and success depends mainly on willingness and skills.

In many cases the comparison with today's Georgia is that "it was better under the communists." There are entire regions where the collapse of the Soviet Union meant not only the disappearance of jobs but also electricity, gas and cheap subsidised food. I have met people who say things are better now, but many do not.

"In many cases the comparison with today's Georgia is that 'it was better under the communists.'"

In Kazakhstan, comparisons with Soviet times also come up constantly, though not in a positive way. Kazakhs still remember how they were not only a minority in their own homeland but second‑class citizens. Russians, Ukrainians and even a few Estonians who had arrived from across the Soviet Union constantly reminded Kazakhs that they should be grateful for being brought "civilisation" and "culture," turning nomadic herders into "civilised" people.

All this came with the suppression of Kazakh culture and language. Islam, central to Kazakh identity to the point where it is sometimes hard to draw a line between being Muslim and being Kazakh, was pushed underground.

Kazakhs themselves say that Kazakh sufism saved Islam and thus Kazakh identity. Since nomadic herders could not regularly attend mosques, a tradition developed where the local religious authority was the oldest man in the family, the aksakal. Thus mosques, mullahs and imams were not critical for being Muslim. Prayer and Islamic customs survived the Soviet era among Kazakhs.

In Moldova, emphasising Soviet heritage is highly political and characteristic of pro‑Russian politicians and their supporters. Moldova shows clearly where cultivating Soviet heritage leads: it brings Russia increasingly into the life of the state and its people.

About half the population of Moldova believes the country has only one path of development — together with Russia, through difficulties toward the stars. There is also an economic reason: Russia is an important market for Moldovan goods, more important than the European Union.

It should also be mentioned that in all the countries above, Russian is the first language used to communicate with foreigners. It is ironic that Georgians like to say Russian is disappearing and English is taking over, but in practice it is very hard to manage outside central Tbilisi and Batumi's tourist areas without Russian.

All this leads to an interesting mental geography. For Estonia and most Estonians, Russia is clearly "the other" country, somewhere beyond the border, with which nothing much connects us anymore and about which we do not know much.

"I would dare say that while Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have mentally turned their backs on Russia, most former Soviet republics have not."

In Moldova, Kazakhstan and Georgia, Russia is "one of us," a foreign country in the same way Estonians tend to view Latvia. As a colleague once told me years ago in Kazakhstan: "For us, the Soviet Union is the Homeland." With a capital letter. In the shadow of that Great Homeland, Russia slips ever deeper into these countries, and the boundary between the Soviet Union and Russia fades — in a positive sense.

A Russian tends to be a different kind of foreigner in these countries than a citizen of any random European state. Georgians, Kazakhs and Moldovans share music with Russians, from Kino to Soviet‑era pop, jokes that everyone understands, well‑known films and even shared terminology — the word "comrade" still appears in Russian conversation, and various coins are still called kopecks.

I would dare say that while Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have mentally turned their backs on Russia, most former Soviet republics have not. Yes, propaganda seeps through every crack here too, and there are those who idealise Russia, but in Estonia there is a clear distance toward Russia. For many Georgians, Kazakhs and Moldovans, by contrast, Russia occupies the same space and world.

And that world shines through everywhere in Georgia, Moldova or Kazakhstan. Russian pop music plays in every second taxi, Soviet pioneer songs sound in children's playgrounds, walls are plastered with posters for concerts by Russian artists, and many people eagerly watch Russian television. Still one of us.

World.title: Turkish Air Force takes over NATO's newly upgraded Baltic air defense mission in Estonia
World.content:
Turkey's air force has been deployed to Estonia for the first time to participate in NATO's newly transformed Baltic air defense mission and will patrol the airspace for the next four months.

At last month's NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, it was decided that the two-decade-old Baltic air policing monitoring mission in Estonia and Lithuania would evolve into an air defense mission from August 1.

The new mission makes it possible to counter aerial attacks by employing NATO's integrated air defense system.

"This should ensure that if, for example, the threat picture changes and there is a need to rapidly bring in additional forces, that will be done. Likewise, all the necessary pre-authorizations for making all possible decisions have already been completed as far in advance as possible," Minister of Defense Hanno Pevkur (Reform) said on Friday.

The four-month rotation timetable for NATO allies has already been agreed upon for the next three years. The minister said air forces are unlikely to get bored, as few regions have similar conditions.

The Turkish Air force will lead the first rotation of the Baltic Air Defense Mission in Estonia from August 1, 2026. Source: EDF/ Siim Verner Teder

"Under previous practice, once, twice, even three times a week they have to go and identify aircraft from a country that is not friendly toward us. In their home countries, as a rule, and if we are talking primarily about, for example, Portugal or Spain, which have served here, or Germany as well, they do not have to constantly identify Russian reconnaissance aircraft or Russian fighter jets flying nearby. The visual contact you get with a Russian fighter jet is not something you can experience in Portugal. Therefore, every country that comes here is certainly in a somewhat special situation," Pevkur told ERR.

The Turkish Air Force contingent at Ämari consists of nearly 80 personnel, including 10 pilots. Five F-16 fighter jets are on round-the-clock standby for takeoff.

"Of course, we are proud to be here under NATO. Our aim and goal is to protect NATO airspace, identify threats in this region, and maintain strong air deterrence," Turkish Air Force pilot Lieutenant Atila Özdemir said.

On Friday, mission medals were awarded to the Portuguese Air Force personnel who flew the last air policing mission in Baltic airspace. Lt. Col. Katrin Tõugjas, commander of the Ämari Air Base, thanked the Portuguese for their "outstanding cooperation" and welcomed the new Turkish contingent.

The Turkish Air Force's deployment will end in November. The Italians took over the mission in Lithuania.

The Turkish Air force will lead the first rotation of the Baltic Air Defense Mission in Estonia from August 1, 2026. Source: EDF/ Siim Verner Teder

World.title: Chevron CFO bullish on Iraq after West Qurna 2, Nassiriya agreements
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Chevron boasts “significant potential” to expand its activities in Iraq over the next decade, according to Chief Financial Officer Eimear Bonner, highlighting the US oil company’s increasing trust in the country’s energy sector after recent deals with Baghdad.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Bonner said that Iraq remained one of Chevron’s top priority markets for future production expansion after the signing of preliminary agreements to pursue negotiations on the massive West Qurna 2 and Nassiriya oil fields.

She added that Chevron has been encouraged by its interaction with Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi and Iraq’s Ministry of Oil while discussions continue and that the corporation is also collaborating with Baghdad on diverse crude export routes to boost Iraq’s long-term energy security.

The statements bolster rising trust among foreign energy corporations after Al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States earlier this month, during which Iraq inked more than $60 billion in investment deals covering energy, infrastructure, banking, and technology.

World.title: Syria joins Saudi Arabia, Jordan in warning Iraq over Iran-backed militias
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Syria has joined Saudi Arabia and Jordan in warning Baghdad that strikes conducted from Iraqi soil against neighboring nations may result in military strikes against the armed groups responsible, according to Syrian military officials cited by regional media.

According to Al Jazeera and the US-funded Al Hurra, a senior Syrian military source said that Damascus will react to any strikes from Iraq by attacking the “terrorist militias” involved inside Iraqi territory.

The purported warning comes amid a steep increase in regional tensions after US-Saudi bombings against Iran-backed militias in Iraq in retaliation for drone assaults on Saudi oil installations, which Riyadh said were conducted from Iraqi territory.

The Iraqi government has frequently said that it would not allow Iraqi land to be used as a launchpad for attacks on neighboring nations.

Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi recently issued an order establishing a comprehensive security strategy aimed at enhancing state authority and preventing armed organizations from endangering regional security.

The new threat puts further pressure on Baghdad, as more neighboring nations indicate they may take direct action if cross-border assaults continue.

Iraqi authorities have attempted to prevent such a situation, claiming that security activities should be overseen by the Iraqi government rather than foreign forces.

Several Iran-backed organizations operating inside Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) are at the heart of the conflict, including Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, Harakat al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.

While the PMF is technically part of Iraq’s security system, some of its sections have strong links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and have been accused by regional governments of carrying out strikes outside of Baghdad’s jurisdiction.

For Iraq, the diplomatic stakes go beyond security.

Baghdad has been attempting to reestablish ties with Syria as part of greater regional economic integration, including talks on resurrecting the old Iraq-Syria oil pipeline to the Mediterranean, which is considered strategically crucial for diversifying Iraq’s export routes outside the Gulf.

The purported Syrian warning comes at a critical moment for Al-Zaidi’s administration, which has spent recent months bolstering relations with Washington, Ankara, Riyadh, and Damascus while portraying Iraq as a secure destination for global investment.

The mounting threats from neighboring Arab governments highlight the importance of Baghdad demonstrating its ability to prevent armed groups from conducting strikes independent of the state.

Failure to do so risks increasing regional military tensions and jeopardizing Iraq’s aspirations to boost commerce, energy cooperation, and infrastructure projects with its neighbors.

The Syrian government has not issued an official warning, and IraqiNews.com has not independently confirmed the statements ascribed to the Syrian military source.

However, the claims reflect rising regional worry that strikes by Iran-backed militias operating from Iraqi soil could further destabilize the area and hamper Iraq’s diplomatic and economic goals.

World.title: Iran-backed militias threaten Iraq’s ties with US and Gulf
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Escalating tensions between Iran-backed militias are providing one of the most serious hurdles yet to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s ambitions to deepen ties with the United States and Gulf states while luring billions of dollars in international investment.

The most recent crisis followed US-Saudi airstrikes on Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq, when Saudi Arabia accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones at oil installations in the kingdom’s Eastern Province.

Riyadh claimed that the operation targeted the militias responsible for the assaults rather than the Iraqi state or its military forces, but Baghdad denounced the strikes as a breach of national sovereignty.

The recent tensions are being fueled by numerous prominent Iran-aligned organizations operating inside Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), notably Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, Harakat al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.

While the PMF is technically part of Iraq’s security apparatus, many of its groups have strong links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and have occasionally conducted operations outside of Baghdad’s chain of command.

Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi responded by calling an emergency meeting of the Ministerial Council for National Security, canceling a planned trip to Saudi Arabia, and announcing a comprehensive security strategy to prevent Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on neighboring countries.

The administration also reiterated its resolve to keep all weapons entirely under state control.

That vow has gained importance after Al-Zaidi’s visit to Washington earlier this month, during which Iraq and the United States reiterated their commitment to completing the US-led coalition operation by the end of September 2026.

During the visit, Al-Zaidi pledged to ensure that all weapons eventually come into the control of the Iraqi state, citing it as a cornerstone of his government’s security strategy and a crucial step toward bolstering Iraq’s sovereignty and stability.

Since entering office, Al-Zaidi has maintained a policy of balancing Iraq’s ties with rival regional and international forces.

During recent travels to Washington, Ankara, and Tehran, he achieved huge investment and cooperation deals totaling tens of billions of dollars in the energy, banking, technology, infrastructure, and industrial sectors.

His administration has also attempted to strengthen connections with Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Turkey, and other Gulf nations via new transportation corridors, energy alliances, and trade agreements aimed at diversifying Iraq’s economy beyond oil and positioning the country as a regional center linking the Gulf to Europe.

According to analysts, Baghdad’s approach is highly dependent on proving that the Iraqi state, rather than armed groups, controls the country’s security and foreign policy.

Continued strikes from Iraqi territory risk eroding the country’s reputation with major regional allies and international investors, at a time when foreign investment has risen after years of turmoil.

The stakes rose when US President Donald Trump said that recent US-Saudi operations against Iran-backed militias were coordinated with the Iraqi government, a claim Baghdad has denied.

Observers believe it reflects rising discontent among Iraq’s leadership with armed groups accused of dragging the nation into regional conflicts that contradict Baghdad’s diplomatic and economic interests.

Al-Zaidi is currently facing the most significant test of his leadership.

Delivering on his promise to place all weapons under state control will be critical not only for Iraq’s internal security but also for maintaining trust with the United States, Gulf Arab states, and international investors, many of whom support many of the country’s largest economic projects.

Baghdad’s dilemma now extends beyond managing ties between Washington and Tehran.

It demonstrates that the Iraqi state possesses both the authority and the political will to prevent Iran-backed militias from using Iraqi territory to launch attacks that risk isolating the country, harming relations with Arab neighbors and the United States, and jeopardizing Iraq’s long-term economic recovery and investment goals.

World.title: Iraq faces growing fiscal strain
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is under increasing financial strain as plummeting oil earnings tighten government budgets, with Health Minister Abdul Hussein al-Mousawi saying that ensuring monthly public-sector wages has become the government’s top priority.

Speaking at a public meeting, al-Mousawi stated that the government requires approximately 10.8 trillion Iraqi dinars ($8.2 billion) per month to pay public-sector salaries, while current monthly oil revenues have fallen to approximately 2.5 trillion dinars, highlighting the growing gap between government obligations and income.

The statements are one of the most direct public acknowledgements by a top Iraqi official of the government’s financial challenges after months of decreased oil prices and fewer export profits.

Iraq’s government finances remain very vulnerable to variations in global energy markets because the vast bulk of public revenue comes from crude oil.

Official figures published this week indicated that oil accounted for over 84% of federal income in the first five months of 2026, but collections decreased by more than one-third compared to the same time the previous year as oil prices and export profits plummeted.

The health minister also warned of financing restrictions in the healthcare sector, citing worries about the supply of medications and the government’s capacity to sustain public services if financial pressures continue.

The fresh warnings follow weeks of increased regional tensions, which disrupted oil markets and added uncertainty to Iraq’s economic prospects.

As OPEC’s second-largest producer, Iraq relies on oil exports to fund wages, pensions, social welfare, and the majority of government expenditure, making the budget susceptible to long-term reductions in crude prices.

Economists have long cautioned that Iraq’s reliance on oil income makes the nation susceptible to external shocks, while a hefty public-sector pay bill constrains the government’s budgetary flexibility.

Previous administrations attempted to diversify income streams via tax changes and non-oil investments, but hydrocarbons remain the economy’s backbone.

The financial pressure comes at a critical time for Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s government, which has been promoting Iraq as a destination for billions of dollars in foreign investment following agreements signed with US, Turkish, and international companies in energy, banking, technology, and infrastructure.

Continued budgetary strain may make it more urgent to accelerate economic reforms, raise non-oil income, and improve public financial management to lessen Iraq’s reliance on petroleum exports.

They also emphasize that preserving investor trust will be contingent on the government’s ability to maintain macroeconomic stability while continuing to fund big development projects.

Despite the present issues, Iraq has large foreign currency reserves, which act as a financial cushion for the government.

However, experts warn that while reserves might help absorb short-term shocks, they are not a substitute for the fundamental changes needed to diversify the economy and reduce its dependence on unpredictable oil earnings.

World.title: Iraq expects record 22 million pilgrims for Arbaeen
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is prepared to welcome around 22 million pilgrims for this year’s Arbaeen pilgrimage, including up to 5 million overseas tourists, in what officials believe to be one of the country’s greatest religious gatherings and a significant boost to tourism and the local economy.

According to Iraqi official data, well over 22 million people are anticipated to attend the annual pilgrimage to the holy city of Karbala, with 4.5 million to 5 million pilgrims coming from outside Iraq.

The government has announced that tens of thousands of volunteers would be deployed to assist pilgrims, and Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has urged officials to boost the number of buses and other transport services to facilitate travel during the festival.

The surge of foreign tourists is projected to have a substantial impact on Iraq’s tourism, hospitality, transportation, and retail industries, with hotels, restaurants, transit operators, and local businesses benefitting from increased demand during the pilgrimage season.

Officials have extended transportation networks in preparation for this year’s pilgrimage, including more rail services, buses, and logistical assistance, as part of larger measures to boost connectivity and promote Iraq’s tourist industry.

The government has increasingly highlighted religious tourism as a crucial pillar of economic diversification, with millions of people visiting the country’s holy sites at Karbala, Najaf, Kadhimiya, and Samarra each year.

According to officials, continuing investment in infrastructure and tourist services will help Iraq become one of the Middle East’s major religious tourism destinations, while also creating jobs and helping local economies around the country.

World.title: Reports: Iraq PM threatened to resign over militia disarmament
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has threatened to resign if Iran-aligned armed groups do not cooperate with his government’s efforts to bring all weapons under state control, according to reports citing political sources, highlighting the growing pressure on Baghdad to address one of its most difficult security challenges.

According to sources, Al-Zaidi warned leaders of Iraq’s Shi’ite Coordination Framework that if armed groups did not react to government efforts to disarm and completely submit to state authority, he would stand down.

IraqiNews.com was unable to independently verify the claims, and the Prime Minister’s office had no immediate response.

According to the sources, Al-Zaidi has been more dissatisfied by what he sees as a lack of cooperation on one of his administration’s fundamental commitments: guaranteeing that all weapons stay solely under the control of the Iraqi government.

The claims came days after US-Saudi airstrikes struck Iran-backed groups in Iraq in response to drone assaults on Saudi oil installations, which Riyadh said were launched from Iraqi territory.

The bombings forced Al-Zaidi to call an emergency security conference, cancel a planned trip to Saudi Arabia, and unveil a new security strategy aimed at preventing Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on neighboring nations.

Armed organizations have emerged as one of Al-Zaidi’s most pressing problems.

Since entering office, he has attempted to solicit billions of dollars in foreign investment with trips to Washington, Tehran, and Ankara, while portraying Iraq as a stable location for oil, infrastructure, and technological projects.

Analysts believe Baghdad’s economic objectives are strongly dependent on its ability to show that the state, not armed groups, controls Iraq’s security strategy.

Repeated strikes conducted from Iraqi territory have strained ties with regional allies and risk weakening investor trust.

According to Western diplomatic sources published by Asharq Al-Awsat, key Iraqi officials, including Al-Zaidi and members of Iraq’s security apparatus, have received threats in connection with the government’s attempts to restrict weaponry outside of state control.

Unlike many regional leaders, Iraq’s prime minister leads by wide political agreement rather than a legislative majority, restricting his power to make unilateral choices.

Major security and political changes usually need agreement among Iraq’s different political blocs.

Al-Zaidi’s biggest power may not be the threat of resignation, but rather the international backing his administration has garnered as a result of recent accords with the United States, Turkey, and other allies.

These agreements, which span energy, finance, technology, and infrastructure, have boosted hopes that Iraq will attract tens of billions of dollars in investment if security improves.

Whether Al-Zaidi can translate that international momentum into domestic reforms will ultimately depend on gaining broader political support for his pledge to keep all weapons under Iraqi state control, which has become one of his government’s most closely watched tests.

World.title: Iraq denies launching strikes from its territory against neighboring nations
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The military spokesperson for the Iraqi commander-in-chief, Sabah al-Numan, confirmed on Thursday that neither a foreign nor local body has presented proof that recent regional drone attacks were launched from Iraqi territory.

In a statement to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), al-Numan urged accusing parties to submit reliable proof, saying that Baghdad has yet to receive such data.

The development comes following statements made by the Saudi Ministry of Defense, alleging that drone attacks targeting key oil infrastructure in the past few days originated in Iraq.

The Iraqi official indicated that the government will neither tolerate unilateral military acts from within its borders nor accept foreign violations of its territorial sovereignty.

Al-Numan’s remarks come a day after the United States and Saudi Arabia launched coordinated airstrikes targeting several bases of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing and injuring many fighters.

The joint operation targeted several logistical and weapons storage locations in different provinces in Iraq, escalating the current regional battle.

The PMF described the joint US-Saudi strike as a dangerous escalation and a clear breach of Iraqi sovereignty.

World.title: Iraqi oil flows to continue via Turkey’s Ceyhan as renewal deal is discussed
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkish sources told Reuters that crude oil shipments from northern Iraq to the Turkish port of Ceyhan will continue while the two countries seek an arrangement to extend the pipeline’s operation for another 12 months.

On July 27, a bilateral agreement that had been in place for decades ended. Despite expectations, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi did not sign a 12-month renewal deal during his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Tuesday.

According to a Turkish official, oil flows via the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, which is Baghdad’s only operational export pipeline, will continue while negotiations for a renewal deal are still in progress.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar recently announced a 12-month extension agreement between the two countries.

During a joint press conference in Ankara, Erdogan stated on Tuesday that Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement as soon as possible.

An extension is intended to provide additional time for discussions on a complete accord. Turkey aims to fully utilize the 1.5 million barrels per day pipeline and consider expanding it to oil fields in southern Iraq.

Turkish data suggests that the pipeline currently transports approximately 170,000 barrels per day.

World.title: Nathula pass border trade resumes after 6 years; traders seek expansion of goods list
World.content:
Border trade through the Nathula Pass in East Sikkim, a key segment of the ancient

connecting India and China, resumed on Saturday after remaining suspended for nearly six years.

A formal reopening ceremony was held at Nathula, with officials from both countries participating in the event.

The trade route had remained closed since 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic and subsequent border tensions between India and China.

Welcoming the resumption of trade, Anil Gupta, General Secretary of the Indo-China Nathula Border Traders Welfare Association, thanked Sikkim Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang for his efforts in facilitating the reopening.

"I extend heartfelt thanks to our Chief Minister, Prem Singh Tamang. This has become possible today solely due to his efforts. For traders who had outstanding dues or stocks stranded on the other side, this is a time of great joy, and everyone is happy," Gupta said.

Traders seek expansion of trade list

While welcoming the resumption of trade, Gupta said the existing list of goods permitted through Nathula needs to be updated to reflect present-day commercial needs.





"The current trading list includes items like horses, sheep and general goods. We believe industrial products relevant to today's times should be included. We have submitted a formal request to the department, and we are hopeful that the government will take a very positive view of this," he said.

Under the existing arrangement, only a limited list of traditional goods is allowed to be traded through the border route.

Traders have long been seeking the inclusion of industrial and other commercially relevant products.

Around 300 traders await passes

Gupta said preparations for the resumption of trade were underway, with authorities verifying applications submitted by traders.

"Around five hundred traders collected forms, and approximately three hundred have submitted them. Verification is underway, and we hope all traders will receive their passes very soon," he said.

The reopening is expected to revive economic activity in the border region and provide relief to traders whose businesses had been affected by the prolonged suspension of cross-border trade. Nathula, located in East Sikkim, is one of the few officially designated border trading points between India and China and has historically served as an important corridor on the ancient Silk Route.

World.title: 'Not met a single parent or student': Rahul Gandhi slams PM Modi over 'forgiving' students video
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress leader

on Saturday hit out at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his remarks on the students who protested against alleged irregularities in the NEET examination.

He accused the Prime Minsiter of failing to acknowledge the suffering of students and their families.

In a post on X, the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha said the real issue was not the conduct of the protesters but the failures of the education system that had left thousands of students uncertain about their futures.

âNothing is more painful than seeing a parent grieve their child. Behind every young life lost is a family carrying pain that will never leave them - and serious questions about a broken education system,â Rahul wrote.

Referring to the controversy surrounding the medical entrance examination, he added, âLeaked papers. Cancelled exams. Years of preparation destroyed overnight. Our students are told to work honestly in a system that is not honest with them.â

Rahul also took aim at the Prime Minister's comments about forgiving students who participated in the protests.

âAnd the Prime Minister has the audacity to speak of âforgivingâ students.





He has not met a single grieving parent. He has not sat with a single student whose future was stolen by a leaked paper. Indiaâs students do not need his forgiveness. They are owed his apology,â he said.

His remarks came a day after PM Modi released a late-night video message on Instagram addressing the protests over the alleged NEET irregularities. The Prime Minister said he was compelled to speak after hearing about the language used against him and his late mother during demonstrations at Jantar Mantar.

PM Modi said he could understand the anguish prevailing in society but urged people to respond with compassion rather than anger. âNot only was I subjected to abusive language at Jantar Mantar, but even my late mother was abused there with filthy language. But abuses never solve anything; let's guide the misguided,â he said.

World.title: 'Honey trap' angle emerges in Bengal Jaish probe; woman arrested from Jharkhand

operative run a 'honey trap' network aimed at collecting personal information about political leaders in the state.

Investigators identified the woman as Arpita Sarkar, who was arrested from Sahibganj district on Friday in connection with the probe into alleged Jaish operative Mohammad Hamim Mondal.

They claimed, as PTI cites, she was in regular contact with Mondal through WhatsApp, and chats between the two have been recovered during the probe.

Alleged honey trap network under scanner

According to STF officials, Sarkar allegedly played a key role in a "honey-trap" network used to lure targets and gather sensitive personal information about influential political leaders in West Bengal.

"Sarkar allegedly played a key role in a 'honey-trap' network used to lure targets as part of the suspected module's activities. Our investigation suggests that the accused attempted to build a network to access sensitive personal information of certain political personalities," an STF official said.

Officials alleged that Mondal used Sarkar to establish contacts with influential political figures and collect personal details about them.





Investigators are now examining whether the information was intended to facilitate future terror attacks or other anti-national activities.

Sarkar has been brought to Purba Bardhaman and is scheduled to be produced before a local court.

World.title: 'In every national security decision, Doval had a role': Amit Shah praises NSA at award ceremony
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Union home minister

on Saturday lauded National Security Advisor (NSA)

for his contribution to India's national security and foreign policy, saying the veteran intelligence officer has played a crucial role behind every major national security decision taken by Prime Minister Narendra Modi since 2014.

Speaking at a function in Pune after presenting the Lokmanya Tilak National Award 2026 to Doval, Shah said the NSA's advice and strategic inputs have been instrumental in strengthening India's security architecture and defence preparedness.

He also said Doval's contribution to India's internal and external security had been so significant that history would reserve "a golden page" for him.

"NSA Ajit Doval has played a great role in strengthening India's foreign policy.

In every decision of PM Modi for national security, Doval has had a 'role and advice' in the background," Shah said.

"Whenever history is written, if anyone analyses internal security and external security, then clearly, for Ajit Doval ji, a golden page will have to be kept reserved; there is no doubt about this," he added.

'First selection' after Modi became PM

Shah said one of the first decisions taken by PM Modi after assuming office in 2014 was appointing Doval as the National Security Advisor, a move he said transformed India's strategic posture.





"Today, India's foreign policy has become a foreign policy with a backbone of steel; no one can deny this. We have, along with self-respect, strengthened our position in the world," Shah said.

Praising Doval's decades-long career in the Intelligence Bureau, Shah said India has emerged as a stronger and more confident nation under Modi's leadership, with Doval making a significant contribution to that transformation.

"After becoming NSA in 2014, Doval helped implement many strategic ideas on the ground and played a major role in modernising India's armed forces, strengthening technology, enhancing operational capability and improving the country's defence preparedness," Shah said.

He added that the Modi government has fundamentally transformed both the defensive and offensive capabilities of the armed forces over the past 12 years, with Doval playing a key role in the process.

Shah also noted that much of Doval's contribution can never be made public because of the confidential nature of intelligence operations.

Recalling his tenure as Gujarat's home minister, Shah narrated how he first interacted with Doval following the Ahmedabad serial bomb blasts. He said then chief minister Narendra Modi had advised Gujarat Police to consult Doval while investigating the attacks.

"I remember Ajit ji had come to my house. The tips he gave resulted in Gujarat Police resolving not just the Ahmedabad bomb blast, but 13 bomb blasts across the country all at once.

This was a very great achievement," Shah said.

Shah invokes Lokmanya Tilak's legacy

The Union home minister also paid tribute to Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, calling him one of the foremost architects of India's freedom movement.

He said Tilak's iconic slogan, "Swarajya is my birthright, and I shall have it," gave a new direction to India's freedom struggle and inspired generations of freedom fighters.

Shah added that the slogan made Indians realise that self-rule was their right and not a favour bestowed by anyone.

Describing Tilak as a fearless journalist, Shah said one could truly understand courage in journalism only by reading the articles published in Kesari, the newspaper founded by the freedom fighter.

"How fearless a journalist can be can only be experienced by reading the articles of Kesari," he said.

Referring to Tilak's role in mobilising people through the public Ganesh and Shivaji festivals, Shah said they laid the foundation for cultural nationalism and that India continues to follow the path envisioned by the freedom fighter.

"India is now moving firmly on the path of cultural nationalism laid down by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and no one can reverse that journey," he said.

Shah further added that Tilak's ideas on nationalism, self-rule and social awakening continue to guide the country and remain relevant for nation-building, particularly for the younger generation.

"When such individuals are honoured, the feeling of gratitude of society towards them is discharged... Today, the Tilak Award that has been conferred upon Ajit Doval ji... for those who live for this country and work for this country, it will become a place of great inspiration," he said.

World.title: Omar Abdullah condemns Kulgam terror attack, says compensation can’t undo families’ suffering
World.content:
Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Saturday (August 1, 2026) condemned the terrorist attack in Kulgam district and said no amount of compensation could undo the damage suffered by families of those who had come there to earn an honest livelihood.

According to officials, Deepak Ratray and Bopinder, both in their 20s, were killed when terrorists attacked a brick kiln in the Kelam area of south Kashmir’s Kulgam district late on Friday evening (July 31, 2026).

Speaking to reporters here after attending an event, he said, “They had come to Kashmir to work. People from outside the state had come here to earn an honest livelihood. Those innocent people were targeted in such a manner. The attack cannot be condemned enough.” He added that no amount of money could undo the impact of the attack or ease the pain and suffering of their families.

“However, this is a small effort from our side to extend some assistance to them during this difficult time,” he added.

CM Abdullah announced an ex gratia relief of ₹10 lakh each for the families of the two migrant labourers from Chhattisgarh who were killed in the terror attack.

The amount is in addition to the immediate assistance of ₹6 lakh each announced by the district administration.

Responding to a question regarding the protest led by him at Jantar Mantar seeking the restoration of statehood for Jammu and Kashmir, Abdullah said the movement would continue until the demand was fulfilled.

He said the demonstration at Jantar Mantar was only the beginning and acknowledged that statehood would not be restored through a one-day protest.

“We know that we are not going to get statehood just by coming to Jantar Mantar for one day. Thousands of students came, and they had to protest for 25 days...(to get their demands met). We too will have to continue this process,” he said.

The CM said the protests would continue in different forms, with some programmes being held in Jammu and Kashmir and others in Delhi.

He said the demand for the restoration of statehood was based on commitments made by the government.

“We are not saying anything for which a promise was not made to us. It was repeatedly said in the Supreme Court and inside the House that Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood would be restored. We are only reminding the Central Government to fulfil its promise,” CM Abdullah said.

On the government’s assurance that no action would be taken against students involved in the recent protests over the NEET question paper leak, Abdullah said a commitment made by the government should be honoured.

“If a promise has been made, then it should be kept. Similarly, the people of Jammu and Kashmir were promised that they would get statehood,” he added.
